s.def: A large beef steak, containing a T-shaped bone.

ety: From its shape, 1920s.

s.def: A lightweight shirt without buttons, usually with short sleeves and no collar. Often made of cotton and frequently bears a picture or slogan.
ex: Many bands make more money from T-shirt sales than from sale of tickets.

s.def: An undershirt.

ety: First attested 1607, of uncertain origin.

s.def: navigational widget in a GUI
A small flap or strip of material attached to or inserted into something, for holding, manipulation, identification, opening etc.
ex: insert tab A into slot B
"His name was written upon a tab within it - Maple White, Lake Avenue, Detroit, Michigan."
He pulls off his belt, cursing as the studs catch in the tabs of his jeans.

s.def: An ear.
A navigational widget, resembling a physical tab, for switching between documents or sets of controls.
The page or form (for example, on a web browser or file manager) associated with such a navigational widget.
ex: How many tabs are open on your browser right now?
That’s the relief I feel when clearing all the tabs in my internet browser. Clicking the crosses like a long line of kisses finally indulged.

s.def: A fast march or run with full kit.
To affix with tabs; to label.
A restaurant bill.
ex: to pick up the tab

s.def: Credit account, e.g., in a shop or bar; slate.
ex: to start a tab
Put this round on my tab, please, barman.

s.def: The cost or bill for anything.
ex: Moreover, at a tab of $9 million, the system's price is about $1 million less than a conventional heating-cooling plant […]

ety: From Old French tabart (“simple sleeveless overtunic; heavy overmantel”), of unknown origin.

s.def: A silk banner attached to a bugle or trumpet.
A sleeveless jerkin or loose overgarment.
ex: The long rows of wheat-shocks marched like soldiers in worn yellow tabards.
This is the point at which someone usually suggests riders wear a numbered, hi-vis tabard.

s.def: A sleeveless garment made of coarse cloth formerly worn outdoors by the common people.
A cape or tunic worn by a knight, emblazoned with the coat of arms of his king or queen on the front.
ex: And thereupon, behold, a knight on a black horse appeared, clothed in jet-black velvet, and with a tabard of black linen about him.

s.def: A similar garment officially worn by a herald and emblazoned with his sovereign's coat of arms.
ex: The heralds in their tabards were marvellous to behold, and a nod from Rouge Croix gave me the keenest gratification.

s.def: A strong fabric consisting of stripes of silk and satin.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic تَبُّولَة (tabbūla).

s.def: A Levantine salad or meze generally consisting of bulgur wheat, chopped tomatoes, parsley, olive oil, and lemon juice.

ety: Mid 17th century French tabis, from Arabic عَتَّابِيّ (ʕattābiyy), ultimately from Arabic الْعَتَّابِيَّة (al-ʕattābiyya), a quarter of Baghdad (named for a Prince عَتَّاب (ʕattāb)) which is associated with the manufacture of a certain type of waved silk. See also taffeta, another type of silk whose name derives from the Persian تافته (tâfta, “woven cloth”) and shares a similar etymological origin.

s.def: A brindled cat.
ex: A wise tabby, a blinking sphinx, watched from her warm sill. Pity to disturb them. Mohammed cut a piece out of his mantle not to wake her.

s.def: A kind of waved silk, usually called watered silk, manufactured like taffeta, but thicker and stronger. The watering is given to it by calendering.
A concrete mixture of lime with shells, gravel, or stones, in equal proportions, with an equal proportion of water. When dry, this becomes as hard as rock.
A woman, irrespective of age, but often used for a young, attractive woman.
An old maid or gossip.
Brindled; diversified in color.
Having a wavy or watered appearance.
ex: a tabby waistcoat

s.def: To give a wavy or watered appearance to (a textile).

ety: From Middle English tabernacle (14th century), from Old French tabernacle, from Latin tabernāculum (“tent, booth, shed”), the diminutive of taberna (“hut, shed”). By surface analysis, taberna + -cle.

s.def: The portable tent used before the construction of the temple, where the shekinah (presence of God) was believed to dwell.
Any temporary dwelling; a hut, tent, or booth.
The Jewish Temple at Jerusalem (as continuing the functions of the earlier tabernacle).
Any portable shrine used in heathen or idolatrous worship.
A sukkah, the booth or 'tabernacle' used during the Jewish Feast of Sukkot.
A small ornamented cupboard or box used for the reserved sacrament of the Eucharist, normally located in an especially prominent place in a church.
A temporary place of worship, especially a tent, for a tent meeting, as with a venue for revival meetings.
Any house of worship, especially a Mormon meetinghouse.
Any abode or dwelling place, or especially the human body as the temporary dwelling place of the soul, or life.
A hinged device allowing for the easy folding of a mast 90 degrees from perpendicular, as for transporting the boat on a trailer, or passing under a bridge.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tābēs.

s.def: A kind of slow bodily wasting or emaciating disease, often accompanying a chronic disease.

ety: From Latin tabescens, present participle of tabescere.

s.def: Wasting away, or becoming emaciated.
ex: He is weak and stinking, tabescent, at the far edge of hope.

ety: From French, from Italian tavolatura, from Latin tabulatura, from tabula.

s.def: A form of musical notation indicating fingering rather than the pitch of notes, commonly used for stringed instruments.
An engraved tablet, or a painting on a wall or ceiling, or sometimes a picture in general.
A division of the skull into two tables.

ety: Inherited from Middle English table, tabel, tabil, tabul, from Old English tabele, tabul, tablu, tabule, tabula (“board”); also as tæfl, tæfel, an early Germanic borrowing of Latin tabula (“tablet, board, plank, chart”). The sense of “piece of furniture” is from Old French table, of same Latin origin; Old English used bēod or bord instead for this meaning: see board. Doublet of tabula and tavla.

s.def: A two-dimensional presentation of data; an enumeration of data or contents.
ex: table of contents, tide table

s.def: item of furniture
Furniture with a top surface to accommodate a variety of uses.
ex: Set that dish on the table over there, please.

s.def: A group of people at a table, for example, for a meal, meeting or game; a meeting at a table.
ex: Time to come to table.
Join us at the table I booked at the restaurant.

s.def: Any of various flat surfaces or items with a planar surface.
To supply (a guest, client etc.) with food at a table; to feed.
ex: 'April 13 1638, Henry Wotton, letter to John Milton At Siena I was tabled in the house of one Alberto Scipioni

s.def: To delineate; to represent, as in a picture; to depict.
ex: c. 1607, Francis Bacon, letter to Tobie Matthew tabled and pictured in the chambers of meditation

s.def: To tabulate; to put into a table or grid.
ex: to table fines

s.def: To put on the table of a commission or legislative assembly; to propose for formal discussion or consideration, to put on the agenda.
To represent a company or organization (at an exposition, fair, etc.), usually at a booth or display.
A list of titles of the parts of a book or document, organized in the order in which the parts appear.
A region of data on a compact disc that describes the contents that follow.
A game or sport (similar to tennis) that involves the hitting of a light plastic ball with rackets (called paddles, or bats in Britain) across a table fashioned like a miniature tennis court.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French tableau, from Old French tablel (“a surface which is used primarily for painting”).

s.def: A striking and vivid representation or scene; a picture.
A vivid graphic scene of a group of people or objects arranged as in a painting or bas relief sculpture.
An arrangement of actors in static positions on stage, having the effect of pointing up a particular moment in the drama, conventionally revealed by opening tableau curtains (known as "tabs").
A two-dimensional array or table of data, usually numbers, of various specific kinds.
A table that shows constraint violations of a list of candidates given an input and a constraint ranking.
Mostly in solitaire card games, but also in other card and board games, the main area, where random cards can be arranged.
A semantic tableau.
A unit of a play, an opera, or a ballet with change of stage setting.
ex: […] several scenes from the first act were consolidated into one tableau […]

ety: From Middle English tabyllcloth, table cloth, tabylle clothe, a partial translation of earlier Middle English bord cloth, bordcloth (“tablecloth”), from Old English bordclāþ, equivalent to table + cloth.

s.def: A cloth used to cover and protect a table, especially for a dining table.
ex: Just across the field stood a small house. In the yard the week's washing was hung out. Among the articles was a red tablecloth.

ety: From table + land.

s.def: A relatively flat region of elevated terrain, particularly in reference to surrounding terrain.
ex: One January day, thirty years ago, the little town of Hanover, anchored on a windy Nebraska tableland, was trying not to be blown away.

ety: Etymology tree Middle English table English table English spoon English tablespoon From table + spoon.

s.def: A large spoon, used for eating food from a bowl.

A unit of volume, the value of which varies regionally; in the US: three teaspoons or one half fluid ounce or roughly 15 ml; in Britain and Canada: exactly 15 ml; in Russia 18 ml; in Australia: four teaspoons or 20 ml.
ex: In Australia, 1 tablespoon equals 20 ml, and there are 4 teaspoons in the Australian tablespoon.

s.def: A spoon too large for eating, usually used for cooking or serving.

ety: From Middle English tablet, from Old French tablete (Modern French tablette), diminutive of table (“table”). Compare English table, -et.

s.def: A slab of clay, stone or wood used for inscription.
A short scripture written by the founders of the Baháʼí Faith.
A pill; a small, easily swallowed portion of a substance in solid form.
ex: Many people take vitamin tablets as a food supplement.

s.def: A block of several sheets of blank paper that are bound together at the top; pad of paper.
ex: Take a full-size writing tablet and follow these steps.

s.def: A tablet computer, a type of portable computer.
A graphics tablet.
A confection made from sugar, condensed milk and butter, produced in flat slabs, with a grainer texture than fudge.
A type of round token giving authority for a train to proceed over a single-track line.
To form (a drug, etc.) into tablets.
A hand-held portable computer in the form of a tablet with a touch screen interface.

ety: From table + top.

s.def: The flat, horizontal upper surface of a table.
A fixed item resembling a table, used for performing skateboarding tricks.
A photograph of an object or product placed on a table.
ex: Photographic greeting cards are usually tabletops.

s.def: Ellipsis of tabletop game.
ex: Some people watch TV, others play tabletops. You might like to work out. The object is to bide your time.

ety: Etymology tree English table Proto-Germanic *warō Proto-West Germanic *waru Old English waru Middle English ware English -ware English tableware From table + -ware.

s.def: The cutlery, crockery and glassware used in setting a table for a meal.

s.def: A compact or compressed version of something; especially something having a popular or sensational nature.
A small, compressed portion of a chemical, drug, food substance, etc.; a pill, a tablet.
ex: One of the compartments was found to contain some forty compressed tabloids, which on analysis proved to be potassium bromide.
‘It's those tabloids!’ Conroy stamped his foot feebly as he blew his nose. ‘They’ve knocked me out.’
"No drops or tabloids or anything of that kind?" "Certainly not; the medicines were kept in my room."

s.def: In the form of a tabloid (noun senses 2 and 2.2): compressed or compact in size.
ex: "The Dairy Maid," an alleged song, is really a recitation; a sort of tabloid sentimental melodrama.

s.def: Resembling the style of journalism generally associated with a tabloid newspaper: appealing to unsophisticated people, sensational, etc.
ex: tabloid journalism

s.def: To express (something) in a compact or condensed manner, especially in the style of journalism generally associated with a tabloid newspaper (appealing to unsophisticated people, sensational, etc.).
To convert (a newspaper) into a tabloid (noun sense 2.2) format.

ety: Borrowed from Tongan tapu (“prohibited, sacred”), from Proto-Polynesian *tapu, from Proto-Oceanic *tabu, from Proto-Eastern Malayo-Polynesian *tambu. Doublet of kapu. First attested in c. 1777. The p in the Tongan source was misheard as b.

s.def: An inhibition or ban that results from social custom or emotional aversion.
ex: It is true indeed that a taboo - in order to be a proper taboo - must not rest in the general mind on argument or reason.
The sharp differentiation of the sexes in our culture was shaped most probably by monogamy and monosexuality and their tabus.

s.def: Something which may not be used, approached or mentioned because it is sacred.

ety: Borrowed from Iranian Persian تَبْریز (tabriz), ultimately from Classical Persian تَبْریز (tabrēz) (see for more information).

s.def: city and county in Iran

A city in Iran, the seat of Tabriz County's Central District and the capital of East Azerbaijan Province. Fourth largest city of Iran with population of about 1,600,000. Historical names: Davrezh, Tavrezh, Tavrez, Tauris.
A county of Iran, around the city.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tabula rāsa (literally “erased tablet”), where the collocation comprised tabula (“wax-covered writing tablet”, noun) + rāsa, feminine singular of rāsus (“scraped, erased, cleaned (of text)”, participial adjective).

s.def: the idea that the mind comes into the world as a blank state
A mind, as of a newborn, free of any impressions, notions, ideas, etc.
ex: Near-synonym: clean slate

s.def: Anything which exists in a pristine state.
ex: Near-synonyms: clean slate, blank slate
In his quest for rehabilitation, Connally is counting on the newspapers' behaving as they normally do: becoming tabulae rasae every 24 hours.
Facebook was a “tabula rasa with carte blanche”, [Yann] LeCun says. “Money was clearly not going to be a problem.”

ety: From Late Latin tabulāris. By surface analysis, tabula + -ar, or, by surface analysis, table + -ar. Compare fabular.

s.def: Organized as a table or list.
ex: In technical communication, don't use prose to present information that lends itself to a tabular presentation.

s.def: Having a flat (planar) horizontal surface at top.
ex: Near-synonym: tablelike
Mesas got their name from being tabular.

s.def: Calculated by means of a table.
ex: tabular artillery direction

s.def: Tending to split into thin flat pieces, as slate does.
ex: The local bedrock is tabular.

s.def: tabular bone

ety: From Late Latin tabulātus (“having a floor; floored”), perfect passive participle of tabulō (“to fit with planks”), from tabula (“board, plank”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂- (a variant of *steh₂- (“to stand”)) + *-dʰlom (a variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting tools or instruments)). Equivalent to table + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To arrange in tabular form; to arrange into a table.
ex: The inevitable deduction from the figures tabulated must be that the material prosperity of the people as a whole is making good progress.

s.def: To set out as a list; to enumerate, to list.
To enter into an official register or roll.
To shape with a flat surface.
A pill, a tablet.
Describing a member of an extinct order of corals, the Tabulata: having tabulae (well-developed horizontal internal partitions within each cell).
A member of the order Tabulata.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tacet (“it is silent”), third-person singular present active indicative form of taceō (“to be silent”). Doublet of tacit.

s.def: An instruction indicating silence on the part of the performers of a piece.

ety: From tacho- + -meter.

s.def: device for measuring rpm
A device for measuring the revolutions per minute (RPMs) of a revolving shaft, as with the driveshaft of an automobile.
A device for measuring or indicating velocity or speed, as of blood, a river, a machine, etc.

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin tachycardia, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (takhús, “swift”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”). By surface analysis, tachy- + -cardia. Compare French tachycardie.

s.def: A rapid resting heart rate, especially one above 100 beats per minute; palpitations.
ex: The heart becomes irritable, there is nervous palpitation, or attacks of paroxysmal tachycardia.

ety: Derived from Ancient Greek ταχυγράφος (takhugráphos). By surface analysis, tachy- (“fast”) + -graphy (“writing”).

s.def: The art and practice of rapid writing.
Stenography or shorthand as done in ancient and medieval times.

ety: From tachy- + -lyte.

s.def: A black, vitreous basalt of volcanic origin.

ety: From tachy- + -meter.

s.def: A surveying instrument for quickly finding distances.
A speed indicator; a tachometer.

ety: Formed as: tachy- + -on, from ταχύς (takhús, “swift”, “rapid”). Coined by American physicist Gerald Feinberg in 1967.

s.def: A hypothetical particle that travels faster than the speed of light.
A flaw in a physical theory that predicts the existence of tachyons or similar paradoxical results. Compare with ghost.

ety: Borrowed from late Middle French tacite, or from Latin tacitus (“that is passed over in silence, done without words, assumed as a matter of course, silent”), from tacere (“to be silent”).

s.def: Implied, but not made explicit, especially through silence.
ex: tacit consent
He does this by way of a tacit reference to Homer.
[…] disengagement represents a tacit rejection of governing institutions and processes, especially among young people, […]

s.def: Not derived from formal principles of reasoning; based on induction rather than deduction.

ety: Back-formation from taciturnity, from Middle English taciturnite, from Latin taciturnitās; or alternatively from French taciturne, likely reinforced by Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).

s.def: Silent; temperamentally untalkative; disinclined to speak.
ex: The two sisters could hardly have been more different, one so boisterous and expressive, the other so taciturn and calm.

ety: From Middle English taciturnite, or alternatively from taciturn + -ity; both ultimately from Latin taciturnitās.

s.def: state of being taciturn
The trait of being taciturn.
ex: Humphries broke out more freely into speech than he had done before, for his usual characteristic was that of taciturnity.
Once he is back on the bench, will Justice Thomas revert to his usual taciturnity?

s.def: Failure to assert a legal right in a way that implies that it is being given up.

ety: From Middle English tak, takke (“hook; staple; nail”), from Old Northern French taque (“nail, pin, peg”), from Frankish *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”), of unknown origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dHgʰ-n-, from the root *déHgʰ- (“to pinch; to tear, rip, fray”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Takke (“bough; branch; twig”), West Frisian takke (“branch”), tûk (“branch, smart, sharp”), Dutch tak (“twig; branch; limb”), German Zacke (“jag; prong; spike; tooth; peak”).

s.def: A loose seam used to temporarily fasten pieces of cloth.
A small nail with a flat head.
A thumbtack.
The lower corner on the leading edge of a sail relative to the direction of the wind.
A course or heading that enables a sailing vessel to head upwind.
A direction or course of action, especially a new one; a method or approach to solving a problem.
ex: So stoutly held to tack by those near North-wales men;
‘I know it all right,’ Big Bil snarled, ‘but knowing and proving are two different tacks.’
I thought that my refusing Barnard would alienate Botha, and decided that such a tack was too risky.

s.def: The maneuver by which a sailing vessel turns its bow through the wind so that the wind changes from one side to the other.
The distance a sailing vessel runs between these maneuvers when working to windward; a board.
A rope used to hold in place the foremost lower corners of the courses when the vessel is close-hauled; also, a rope employed to pull the lower corner of a studding sail to the boom.
Any of the various equipment and accessories worn by horses in the course of their use as domesticated animals.

ety: From Middle English takel (“gear, apparatus”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German takel (“ship's rigging”), perhaps related to Middle Dutch taken (“to grasp, seize”). Akin to Danish takkel (“tackle”), Swedish tackel (“tackle”). More at take.

s.def: A device for grasping an object and an attached means of moving it, as a rope and hook.
A block and tackle.
Clothing.
Equipment (rod, reel, line, lure, etc.) used when angling.
Equipment, gear, gadgetry.
A play where a player attempts to take control over the ball from an opponent, as in rugby or football.
A play where a defender brings the ball carrier to the ground.
Any instance in which one person intercepts another and forces them to the ground.
An offensive line position between a guard and an end: offensive tackle; a person playing that position.
The penis.

ety: From tack + -y.

s.def: Of a substance, slightly sticky.
ex: This paint isn't dry yet; it's still a bit tacky.

s.def: Shabby, dowdy in one's appearance or dress.
Of low quality.
ex: That market stall sells all sorts of tacky ornaments.

s.def: Gaudy or flashy.
In poor taste.
ex: That was a tacky thing to say.

s.def: Alternative form of tackey.

ety: Borrowed from French tact, following a semantic shift from earlier tact (“sense of touch; feeling”), borrowed from Latin tāctus (“touched”). The borrowing was likely influenced by earlier English tact (“sense of touch; feeling”), which was a parallel borrowing directly from the Latin.

s.def: Sensitive mental touch; special skill or faculty; keen perception or discernment; ready power of appreciating and doing what is required by circumstances; the ability to say the right thing and avoid statements that will give offence or pain even if true.
ex: By the use of tact, she was able to calm her jealous husband.
I used tact when I told my fat uncle that his extra weight made him look better.
A tact which surpassed the tact of her sex as much as the tact of her sex surpassed the tact of ours.

s.def: Propriety; manners (etiquette).
The sense of touch; feeling.
ex: Did you suppose that I could not make myself sensible to tact as well as sight?
Now, sight is a very refined tact.

s.def: The stroke in beating time.
A verbal operant which is controlled by a nonverbal stimulus (such as an object, event, or property of an object) and is maintained by nonspecific social reinforcement (praise).
ex: Skinner (1957) saw such tacts as responses that are reinforced socially.

s.def: To use a tact (a kind of verbal operant).
Clipping of tactic.

ety: From tact + -ful.

s.def: Possessing tact; able to deal with people in a sensitive manner.

s.def: A maneuver used against an enemy.
A maneuver, or action calculated to achieve some end.
A sequence of moves that limits the opponent's options and results in an immediate and tangible advantage, typically in the form of material.

s.def: Of or relating to tactics.
ex: As in the 1-0 win against Norway in Oslo, this was an England performance built on the foundations of solid defence and tactical discipline.

s.def: Of or relating to military operations that are smaller or more local than strategic ones.
ex: tactical nuclear weapon

s.def: Adroit, skilful or ingenious.
Having a military appearance, typically with accessories such as a bipod, adjustable stock, detachable magazine or black coloration.
A combinator of proof tactics.
A private war reenactment event involving mock battles or skirmishes.

ety: Either borrowed from French tacticien or derived as tactic + -ian.

s.def: A person skilled in the planning and execution of tactics.
plural of tactic
The military science that deals with achieving the objectives set by strategy.
The employment and ordered arrangement of forces in relation to each other.
A system of mode or procedure.
ex: scare tactics

ety: Borrowed from Middle French tactile, from Latin tactilis (“that may be touched, tangible”), from tangere (“to touch”).

s.def: Tangible; perceptible to the sense of touch.
ex: tactile method of reading

s.def: Used for feeling.
Of or relating to the sense of touch.
ex: The delicacy of the tactile sense varies on different parts of the skin; it is greatest on the forehead, temples and back of the forearm.
tactile illusion

s.def: Prone to touching people or things.

ety: Etymology tree English tact Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der. Proto-Germanic *leusaną Proto-Germanic *lausaz Proto-Germanic *-lausaz Proto-West Germanic *-laus Old English -lēas Middle English -les English -less English tactless From tact + -less.

s.def: having no tact; unaware or intentionally inconsiderate of someone else's feelings
ex: It was tactless of you not to attend your sister's wedding.

ety: 1877, ‘young or small child’, probably a shortened form of tadpole. The extended meaning ‘small amount’ is first recorded 1915.

s.def: A small amount; a little bit.
ex: Could you lean the picture to the left just a tad more?

s.def: A street boy; an urchin.

ety: From Middle English tadpolle, taddepol, equivalent to toad + poll (“head”).

s.def: toad or frog larva
A young toad or frog in its larval stage of development that lives in water, has a tail and no legs, and, like a fish, breathes through gills.
The aquatic larva of any amphibian.
ex: salamander tadpole

s.def: A type of cargo bike that has two wheels in front and one in back.
A child's basic drawing of a human being, having a detailed head but only sticks for the body and limbs.
A small child.
ex: Shouldn't you tadpoles be in bed?

s.def: An insignificant person.
ex: Woman's voice: You impudent imp! You tadpole! You shrimp!
“[H]ere's this Tooralooral tadpole of a Mayor shovin' his nose into the business and arrestin' our Puddin' without rhyme or reason.”

ety: Borrowed from Korean 태권도(跆拳道) (taegwondo).

s.def: A martial art from Korea, known for its elaborate kicking techniques. The sparring aspect is a recognised Olympic sport.
ex: Khudadadi, originally from Afghanistan but now living and training in France, won bronze in the taekwondo women’s K44 -47kg category in Paris.

ety: From Portuguese tael, from Malay tahil. Doublet of tahil.

s.def: Any of several units of measure used in China and elsewhere in eastern Asia, approximately 40 grams, and metricated in Mainland China as exactly 50 grams.
Any of several monetary units equal to the equivalent weight in silver.
Leung, a traditional unit of weight, in modern usage legally defined as 1/16 of a catty or kan (斤) or 0.0377993638 kilograms

ety: From Latin taenia, from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “ribbon, tape”).

s.def: A ribbon worn in the hair in ancient Greece.

s.def: The quality, state, or characteristic of being tasteless.

ety: From Middle English taster; equivalent to taste + -er.

s.def: An object in which, or by which, food or drink is tasted, such as a small cup or spoon.
ex: A flight of tasters was served to the people who would vote on the next soda flavor to be released.

s.def: Someone who tastes something; especially, either (1) to check its quality (in food science, winemaking, etc.) or (2) as a security measure to prevent assassination of a protectee.
ex: Big companies such as P&G or Kraft Heinz employ or contract with professional tasters who help with product development.
Being a cook for protectees also entails being a taster for them.

s.def: A kind of zooid situated on the polyp-stem of certain Siphonophorae, resembling the feeding zooids, but destitute of mouths.
A sample of something bigger or grander intended for future use.
ex: The Kraft Heinz exhibit at the trade fair was a taster of new snack products set to hit the market soon.
The Samsung exhibit at the trade fair was a taster of new consumer electronic products set to hit the market soon.

s.def: A person who is, by genetic makeup, able to taste phenylthiocarbamide.
A unit of volume equivalent to a Roman cyathus.

ety: From taste + -y. The Philippine sense is due to a genericized trademark from Taystee Bread Company, a defunct American company.

s.def: Having a pleasant or satisfying flavor.
ex: You could make this tasty meal for breakfast.

s.def: Having or showing good taste; tasteful.
ex: These items will make an attractive and tasty display.
we wait until the palace is half-way up, and then we pay some tasty architect to run us up an ornamental mud hovel, right against it

s.def: Skillful; highly competent.
Potentially violent.
Having good taste; tasteful.
ex: But you must wear pink, my dear; that blue thing as your aunt Glegg gave you turns you into a crowflower. Jane never was tasty.

s.def: Appealing; when applied to persons, sexually appealing.
ex: Country fans probably remember Stu best for a tasty tune he wrote and recorded but didn't want released.

s.def: Something tasty; a delicious article of food.
ex: The mate had procured other tasties too, olives and such, for later in the evening.
Sean then made up the most delicious pâté to have with biscuits and various other tasties.

s.def: A loaf of bread.

ety: From Hindi टाट (ṭāṭ, “thick canvas”).

s.def: Cheap and vulgar tastelessness; sleaze.
Cheap, tasteless, useless goods; trinkets.
Gunny cloth made from the fibre of the Corchorus olitorius (jute).
To make (something by) tatting.
Clipping of tatting.
ex: She's so swishy in her satin and tat / In her frock coat and bipperty-bopperty hat

s.def: A pony.
A tattoo.
ex: Now give me my cable, fast food, four-by's, tats, right away I want it now.
Me and my thugs clock G's, sippin' naughty thangs. Real as these tats on my body, and it's Killuminati.

s.def: To apply a tattoo.
ex: 2016 May 5, Fifth Harmony, “Write on Me”, 7/27, Epic Records, Sysco Music Write on me / Love the way you tat me up

s.def: Alternative form of tatt (“a die, especially one that is loaded”).
Alternative form of tatty (“kind of woven mat or screen”).

ety: From French Tataouine, from Arabic تَطَاوِين (taṭāwīn), from Tunisian Berber tiṭṭawin (“springs”).

s.def: A city in southern Tunisia.

ety: From Old Turkic 𐱃𐱃𐰺 (t¹t¹r¹). More at Tatars. Doublet of Tartar and tartare.

s.def: An agglutinative language belonging to the Altai group of Turkic languages. It is an official language of Tatarstan. There are some eight million speakers spread across Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia.
Tartary.
person
A person belonging to one of several Turkic ethnic groups identified or identifying as "Tatar" in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia.
Of or relating to the people or culture of Tatars.
ex: Tatar customs

ety: From Ukrainian Татарбуна́ри (Tatarbunáry).

s.def: A city in Odesa Oblast, Ukraine.

ety: Transliteration of Russian Татарста́н (Tatarstán). By surface analysis, Tatar + -stan.

s.def: A republic and federal subject of south-central Russia. Official name: Republic of Tatarstan. Capital: Kazan.

ety: From Middle English tater, from Old Norse tǫturr, from Proto-Germanic *tat(t)uraz (“tuft, patch”). Cognate with Icelandic tötur (“rag, tatter”).

s.def: A shred of torn cloth; an individual item of torn and ragged clothing.
ex: You can’t – you shan’t – you don’t – you won’t – you thing of rag and tatter, O!

s.def: To destroy an article of clothing etc. by shredding.
To fall into tatters.
A person engaged in tatting.
To go at great speed.

ety: First attested circa 1608. An early spelling was tatter-de-mallion, rhymed with Italian. The first part of the word is tatter; the origin of the second part is uncertain; Ebenezer Cobham Brewer suggested it might be from de maillot (“shirt”).

s.def: Tattered.
ex: For the same reason the kings of Europe could not resist the tatterdemalion soldiers of the Convention.
Thus, too, we have the woman social reformer, trailing along ridiculously behind a tatterdemalion posse of male utopians, each with something to sell.

s.def: A person with tattered clothing.
ex: Then it wasn’t worth while sending to Neufchâtel for the keeper of a cookshop! And for whom? For cowherds! tatterdemalions! [translating va-nu-pieds]
Rags mounted guard over the treasure. Virtue rendered these tatterdemalions resplendent.

ety: From Middle Dutch tatelen, tateren (“to babble, chatter”) (modern Dutch tatelen, tateren (“to talk, chatter”)), originally imitative. The word is cognate with Saterland Frisian tätelje (“to talk nonsense, babble”), Middle Low German tāteren, tadderen (“to babble, chatter”) (whence modern German Low German tatern (“to chatter”)), Low German tateln, täteln (“to cackle, gabble”). Compare also Middle English dadel, dadull (“tattling, gossip”), and its alteration twaddle.

s.def: To chatter; to gossip.

Often said of children: to report incriminating information about another person, or a person's wrongdoing in an annoying fashion, usually to a person in a position of authority over the accused person; to tell on somebody.
To speak like a baby or young child; to babble, to prattle; to speak haltingly; to stutter.
A tattletale.
ex: We agree on almost nothing, everything is a battle / Every secret from him is kept, his rep is being a tattle

s.def: Often said of children: a piece of incriminating information or an account of wrongdoing that is said about another person.
Idle talk; gossip; (countable) an instance of such talk or gossip.

ety: From tattle + -er.

s.def: One who tattles (notifies authorities of illicit behavior) or is inclined to do so; a tattletale.
ex: My sister is a big tattler; she always tells Mommy when I hit her!

s.def: Either of two similar bird species in the shorebird genus Heteroscelus (Tringa in some taxonomies).
A device fitted to a vehicle to measure mileage etc.
ex: A few truck drivers griped drowsily about the tattlers in their cabs which graphed the mileage per hour per day.
Electronic monitors (black box, tattlers) help to define the actions of the driver during normal and emergent operation of the EMS unit.

ety: From tattle + tale.

s.def: telltale; giveaway
One who tattles (reports others' wrongdoings), often a child seeking attention.
One who gossips, often for the sake of attention.
To act as a tattletale; to tell on; to give away, reveal, or expose.

ety: From earlier tattaow, tattow, a borrowing from a Polynesian language, e.g. Samoan tatau (“tattoo; to tap, to strike”).

s.def: An image made on a body part, usually the skin with ink and a needle.
ex: His shirt sleeves were turned up, so upon his brawny arms his tattooes were visible.

s.def: A method of decorating a body part, usually the skin, by inserting colored substances under the surface with a sharp instrument (usually a solenoid-driven needle).
To apply a tattoo to (someone or something).
ex: She made Silas tattoo an anchor on her arm like his

s.def: To hit the ball hard, as if to figuratively leave a tattoo on the ball.
ex: Jones tattoos one into the gap in left; that will clear the bases.

s.def: A signal played five minutes before taps (lights out).
ex: Study goes on until tattoo, which, when Pops was at the Point, was sounded at 9.30, followed by taps at 10.

s.def: A signal by drum or bugle ordering soldiers to return to their quarters.
A military display or pageant.
A rhythmic tapping.
ex: the right hand became restless and began to beat out a silent tattoo upon the tabletop

s.def: To tap rhythmically on, to drum.
A pony of a certain breed from India.

ety: From tattoo + artist.

s.def: A person who draws tattoos on others.
Having one or more tattoos.
ex: The man was so heavily tattooed that it was almost impossible to find any bare skin on his body.
A copiously tattooed young man in a blue jumpsuit sits mansplayed across from her, shackled to the rail on his side of the hallway, staring at Penny.

ety: From Middle French tanter (“to tempt, try, provoke”), variant of Old French tempter (“to try”). Doublet of tempt.

s.def: To make fun of (someone); to goad (a person) into responding, often in an aggressive manner.
ex: John taunts his brother to reveal his hiding spot.

s.def: A scornful or mocking remark; a jeer or mockery.
Very high or tall.

ety: Borrowed from French taupe, from Latin talpa (“mole”). Doublet of talpa.

s.def: A dark brownish-grey colour, the colour of moleskin.
Of a dark brownish-grey colour.
ex: At five o'clock the patch of daylight above the red-lighted exit door turned taupe, as though a gray curtain had been flung across it; […]
In the front room, on an old taupe overstuffed sofa, the head of the house lay in a blanket bathrobe, […]

ety: From Latin Taurica, from Ancient Greek Ταυρῐκή (Taurĭkḗ).

s.def: An ancient geographic region and peninsula, the name used by the Greeks and Romans for the modern Crimean Peninsula in Eastern Europe, internationally recognized as part of Ukraine but occupied by Russia.

ety: From Latin taurīnus, from taurus (“bull”).

s.def: Pertaining to a bull; bull-like.
ex: I am the Ionian Minotaur, the mightiest Of all Europa’s taurine progeny— I am the old traditional Man-Bull;

s.def: An amino-sulfonic acid, NH₂CH₂CH₂SO₃H, that has regulatory functions in mammals.

ety: From Revived Ancient Greek ταυροκαθάψια (taurokathápsia), variant of ταυροκάθαψις (taurokáthapsis), from ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”) + κάθαψις (káthapsis). Apparently coined by Arthur Evans, the excavator of Knossos, in ca. 1910.

s.def: Bull-leaping, as depicted in Bronze Age art, especially from Minoan Crete.

ety: From Latin Taurus (from taurus (“bull”)), from Ancient Greek Ταῦρος (Taûros) (compare Aramaic תּוֹר (tor), Arabic ثَوْر (ṯawr)), ultimately originating with Sumerian 𒄞𒀭𒈾 (GU₄.AN.NA, “Bull of Heaven; constellation Taurus”) . Latin taurus (“bull”) is a doublet of steer, tur, Tavros, and Tarvos.

s.def: A constellation of the zodiac traditionally figured in the shape of a bull and containing the star Aldebaran.
The zodiac sign for the bull, ruled by Venus and covering April 21 - May 21 (tropical astrology) or May 16 - June 15 (sidereal astrology).
Someone with a Taurus star sign.
An automobile model produced by the Ford Motor Company (1986-present).
A mountain range in southern Anatolia, almost 4000 metres high and running parallel to the Mediterranean coast

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English taught [and other forms], Early Middle English tohte, towehte (“strained, stretched; distended; tight; firm”), probably from tough, touth, touʒth, toʒt (“powerful, strong; fierce, violent; not tender, tough; hardy, resilient; steadfast, stout; difficult to do or endure”) and possibly influenced by togen, towen, past participle of ten (“to extend, stretch out; to drag, haul, pull, tow, tug”) (modern English tee (“(obsolete) to draw, lead; to draw away…

s.def: Under tension, like a stretched bowstring, rope, or sail; tight.
ex: The pressure pad which holds the film taut as it passes the reproducing light beam must apply just the right amount of pressure.
The cord goes taut, tauter, tautest, till down she trips and Adam has a good laugh.
As Red played the intro, he allowed himself a passing glance at her. She was at the back of the crowd, face taut.

s.def: Of a body, muscle, etc., not flabby; firm, toned.
ex: I watched him from the side as he strode along. His walk was quite different; his face too looked tauter.

s.def: Of a person, having a lean, strong body.
Of music, writing, etc., containing only relevant parts; brief and controlled.
ex: If he curbs his swing a little and gets something crisper and tauter in his methods he may yet be very good.
Quick action and dialogue create a taut story, although it is illustration that shapes the characters.

s.def: Experiencing anxiety or stress.
ex: His outward appearance was calm, but inside he was very taut.

s.def: Of a sailor, ship, etc., neat and well-disciplined.
ex: In the tautest schooner that ever swam / He rides at anchor at Anisquam.
You've secured the neatest, trimmest, tautest little craft that ever man could wish to be commander of.

s.def: Strong; uncompromising.
To make taut; to tauten, to tighten.
ex: Men come down to the bare nail / suffer or inflict pain // life demands degradation / tauts the thread that hangs us all: [...]

ety: From taut + -en.

s.def: To make taut; to taut.
ex: Tauten the rope.

s.def: To become taut.
ex: The rope tautened.

ety: From tautology + -ical.

s.def: Of, relating to, or using tautology.
Using repetition or excessive wordiness; pleonastic or circumlocutionary.

ety: From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología) from ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”). By surface analysis, tauto- + -logy.

s.def: Redundant use of words, a pleonasm, an unnecessary and tedious repetition.
ex: It is tautology to say, "Forward Planning".

s.def: An expression that features tautology.
ex: The expression "raze to the ground" is a tautology, since the word "raze" includes the notion "to the ground".
Pure mathematics consists of tautologies, analogous to ‘men are men’, but usually more complicated.

s.def: A statement that is true for all truth values of its propositional variables.
A statement that is true for all truth values of its Boolean atoms.

ety: From Middle English taverne, from Old French taverne (“wine shop”), from Latin taberna (“inn”). Doublet of taberna and taverna.

s.def: bar
A restaurant or bar.
A building containing a bar licensed to sell alcoholic drinks, and offering sleeping accommodations for travelers.
ex: At one of the way-stations on his long journey a barmaid at a tavern speaks to Gilgamesh and tries to give him common sense on the human condition.

ety: From Middle English tawen, from Old English tawian (“to do, make”), from Proto-West Germanic *tawōn, a variant of Proto-West Germanic *tauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *tawjaną (“to make, prepare”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂- (“to tie to, secure”). Cognate with Dutch touwen (“to rope, tether, curry”), Dutch tuien (“to fasten with ropes”), German Tau (“rope, hawser, cable”), Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (taujan, “to make, prepare”). Related to tool and possibly to tether.

s.def: To prepare or dress, as hemp, by beating; to tew.
To beat; to scourge.
To dress and prepare, as the skins of sheep, lambs, goats, and kids, for gloves, etc., by imbuing them with alum, salt, and other agents, for softening and bleaching them.
Tawed leather.
A favorite marble in the game of marbles.
ex: Near the timberyard a squatted child at marbles, alone, shooting the taw with a cunnythumb.

s.def: A line or mark from which the players begin a game of marbles.
A dance partner.
ex: Walk around your corner; see-saw around your taw.

s.def: A favorite person; beloved, partner, spouse.
To shoot a marble.
The 22nd and last letter of many Semitic alphabets/abjads, including Phoenician, Aramaic, Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic.

ety: Shortened from tawdry lace; originally a corruption and rebracketing of Saint Audrey lace (from Old English Æðelþrȳð). The lace necklaces sold to pilgrims to Saint Audrey fell out of fashion in the 17th century, and so tawdry was reinterpreted as meaning “cheap” or “vulgar”.

s.def: Tawdry lace.
Anything gaudy and cheap; pretentious finery.
Of clothing, appearance, etc., cheap and gaudy; showy.
ex: It was all cheap and incredibly tawdry, from the festoons of paper roses on the walls to the flash of paste jewels in make-believe crowns.

s.def: Of a character, behavior, or situation, etc., unseemly, base, mean-spirited, shameful.
ex: The woman's passion by his side seemed suddenly tawdry and unreal, the seeking of her lips for his something horrible.

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English tauni, tawne (“having a brownish-orange colour”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman taune, tawné, and Old French tané, tanné, tanney (“of a tan colour”), an adjective use of the past participle of taner (“to turn hide into leather, tan”), from tan (“pulped oak bark used to tan leather, tanbark”), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)dʰnwos, *(s)dʰonu (“fir”). The -aw-…

s.def: Of a light brown to brownish orange colour; orangey brown tinged with gold.
ex: [P]erhaps they metamorphose themselves into a tawny squirrel that scampers away and mocks you from the topmost bough.
They fell a-twittering among themselves once more, and this time their intoxicating babble was of violet seas, tawny sands, and lizard-haunted walls.
I never thought I'd meet a girl like you / With auburn hair and tawny eyes

s.def: To cause (someone or something) to have a light brown to brownish orange colour; to tan, to tawn.
ex: The General stares into the sandstorm churned up by all that movement. Like a curtain draped across the world, tawnying the October sky.

s.def: To become a light brown to brownish orange colour; to tan, to tawn.
ex: [C]olheita is actually a tawny Port from a single vintage. In other words, it has aged (and softened and tawnied) in wood for many years.

s.def: A light brown to brownish orange colour.
ex: Despise not my discolour'd look: / This tawny from the sun I took.
'Gad, if Miss S. will have me, I'm her man. I ain't particular about a shade or so of tawny.

s.def: Something of a light brown or brownish orange colour (particularly if it has the word tawny in its name).
ex: TAWNY. A bullfinch. Somerset.

s.def: In full tawny port: a sweet, fortified port wine which is blended and matured in wooden casks.
A fabric of a light brown to brownish orange colour.
A person with skin of a brown colour.
ex: The Tavvnies among vvhom vve came, have VVatered our Soyl, vvith the Blood, of many Hundred of our Inhabitants.

s.def: Tawny frogmouth.
Tawny owl.
Any member of the species Strix aluco of strigid owls, of Europe, western Asia, and the Middle East.
Anthus campestris, a medium-to-large passerine bird that breeds in much of temperate Europe and Asia, and northwest Africa.

ety: From Middle English taxe, from Middle French taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa, from Latin taxō (“to appraise, value, estimate; (medieval) to tax”). Doublet of task. Displaced native Old English gafol, which was also the word for “tribute” and “rent”.

s.def: Money or goods collected by a government (or an entity to whom the government has delegated this power, e.g. in tax farming) to fund itself and its services, for example by levying a charge on income, purchases (sales), property or harvest, other than that money which is collected by the government…

A charge (of money, food, labor, etc) collected by a person, organization, etc; something required (exacted) from someone who is (really or notionally) under the control of the taxer, such as a contribution or service.
ex: Flie far from hence All private taxes, immodest phrases, What e'r may but shew like vicious.

s.def: A burdensome demand
ex: a heavy tax on time or health
The extent of the traffic is a tax on the existing yard in the area at Frodingham, the busiest in the District.

s.def: To impose and collect a tax from (a person or company).
ex: Some think to tax the wealthy is the fairest.
Taxing the food and chemical industries, which make billions off our food consumption, could be another way to generate revenue for the program.

s.def: To impose and collect a tax on (something).
ex: Some think to tax wealth is destructive of a private sector.

s.def: To make excessive demands on.
ex: Do not tax my patience.
But patent applications are increasingly accompanied by volumes and volumes of data on DVD, which taxes the resources of the patent office.

s.def: To accuse.
To examine accounts in order to allow or disallow items.
The illegal reduction of paying tax, especially by making a false declaration of income etc.

ety: Compound of tax + haven.

s.def: A jurisdiction that levies low tax rates on certain economic activities, especially to attract wealthy individuals and foreign businesses.

A declaration of income etc. for tax purposes: a report of income, deductions, contributions, and related financial information filed by a taxpayer with a national or local tax authority, used by the authority to determine the amount of taxation, usually consisting of forms completed by the taxpayer

ety: From Middle English taxacioun, from Anglo-Norman taxacion, from Latin taxātio (“rating, appraisal”). By surface analysis, tax + -ation.

s.def: The act of imposing taxes and the fact of being taxed.
A particular system of taxing people or companies
The revenue gained from taxes.
ex: Less than one-tenth of the taxation is spent on public improvements of any kind […]

ety: From taxis

s.def: A primitive feature of grammar, akin to a phoneme in phonology; a small linguistic feature, such as selection, order, or phonetic modification.
ex: Run! is formed by two taxemes: an infinitive verb and an exclamative toneme

s.def: Alternative spelling of tax-free.

ety: From tax + gatherer.

s.def: One who collects taxes or revenues; a tax collector.

ety: Shortened from taximeter cab, taximeter (“automatic meter that records distance and fare”) from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (whence also English taxameter), coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”). More at tax, task. The aviation sense originally derived from a slang term for training aircraft used for practicing ground operations, which were said to drive around the airfield like a taxicab, and subsequently applied to all aircraft ground movements.

s.def: A vehicle that may be hired for single journeys by members of the public, particularly one with an automated meter to calculate the fare.
ex: I cabbed a package downtown in my father's taxi.
"Taxi," he called. And when one pulled up to the curb with screeching brakes he ordered, "The nearest restaurant."
[Sobbing uncontrollably] I thought I could make it work between us because you looked a bit like a man. TAXI!

s.def: An aircraft used for practicing ground manoeuvres.
ex: Capt. Dawes and Bellairs were out with the Deperdussin taxi, and also with the brevet machine, rolling.
Mr. E. B. Bauman (new pupil) joined school and had first lesson on No. 2 taxi.

s.def: The movement of an aircraft across an airport's surface under its own power; a phase of aircraft operation involving this movement.
ex: During taxi, the flaps and slats are extended and the second engine (if not already running) is started.
Seat belts must be kept fastened during taxi, takeoff, turbulence, and landing.

s.def: Synonym of shared taxi.
To move an aircraft on the ground under its own power.
ex: taxi down the runway

s.def: To travel by taxicab.
ex: [H]e had taxied to the waterfront bent upon a business in which nostalgia had no part[.]

s.def: A person who drives a taxicab.
A designated place in a street, railway station, airport etc where taxicabs line up to wait for passengers.

ety: Shortened from taximeter cab, equivalent to taxi + cab.

s.def: Synonym of taxi, a vehicle available for public hire for single journeys, particularly one using a taximeter to automate fare calculation.
To travel by taxicab.

ety: Borrowed from French taxidermie, from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”, “order”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Analysable as taxi- + derm- + -y.

s.def: The art of stuffing and mounting the skins of dead animals for exhibition in a lifelike state.

ety: Borrowed from French taximètre, from German Taxameter, coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to touch, handle”).

s.def: A device installed in a taxicab that calculates the fare based upon distance travelled and waiting time.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement, order”).

s.def: The directional movement of an organism in response to a stimulus.
The manipulation of a body part into its normal position after dislocation or fracture.
The arrangement of the parts of a topic.
arrangement or ordering generally, as in architecture or grammar
A brigade in an Ancient Greek army.
plural of taxi
third-person singular simple present indicative of taxi

ety: From taxi + way.

s.def: A road or path within an airport designated for the taxiing of aircraft connecting the runways with ramps, hangars, terminals and other facilities.

ety: Borrowed from French taxonomie. By surface analysis, taxo- + -nomy.

s.def: The science of finding, describing, classifying and naming organisms.
The science, technique, or process used to make a classification.
ex: Holonym: ontology (relational rather than solely hierarchical)

s.def: A classification; especially, a classification in a hierarchical system.
ex: At the petabyte scale, information is not a matter of simple three- and four-dimensional taxonomy and order but of dimensionally agnostic statistics.

ety: From tax + payer.

s.def: A person who is subject to, liable for, or pays tax.
ex: The bank was bailed out by the taxpayer.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic تَيَمُّم (tayammum).

s.def: The wiping of one's face and hands against dust, sand or a clean physical object in place of wudhu for the bereft or bedridden.

ety: Etymology tree Latin tālea Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Late Latin tāliō Old French taillierder. Old French tailleorder. Anglo-Norman taillourbor. Middle English taillour English tailorder. English Taylor From tailor. Doublet of Tailor.

s.def: A unisex given name transferred from the surname; variant form Tayler.
An English and Scottish surname originating as an occupation; variant form Tailor.
ex: One of the Louisville detectives who fatally shot Breonna Taylor during a botched raid is appealing his termination this week.

s.def: A surname from Irish Táilliúir (“tailor”) [in turn originating as an occupation].

ety: Borrowed, via Spanish tayra or Portuguese taira, from Old Tupi eîrara. (Compare Portuguese irara, Spanish irará, eirá, connected to Paraguayan Guarani eíra (“honey”), a food the animal is fond of, whence also Portuguese papa-mel, another vernacular name.)

s.def: A South American omnivore, Eira barbara, allied to the grison, with a long thick tail.

ety: 1650s, in sense of building, from Late Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós, “pertaining to building”), from Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn, “carpenter, joiner, maker”), from Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- (“to make”) (from which also texture). ety: From Morris Michtom, the owner of a candy store in Brooklyn N.Y., who made the first “Teddy Bear” in the year 1902 in honor of then American President Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt when he had heard that he had refused to shoot a bear cub on one of his hunting trips.

ety: English tedi(um) + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

ety: From Middle English tediosenes, tediousenesse, tediousnesse, tedusnes, teduysnes, tedyousnes; equivalent to tedious + -ness.

ex: [B]revity is the soul of wit, And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes[.]

ety: From Latin taedium, from taedēre (“to weary”).

s.def: Boredom or tediousness; ennui.
ex: Yet active life was the genuine soil for his virtues; and he sometimes suffered tedium from the monotonous succession of events in our retirement.

ety: * From Middle English, from Old English te, from Latin tē (the name of the letter T). * (computing): By analogy with a T-shaped pipe that sends fluids in two directions.

ety: From Middle English temen (“to bear, to support”), from Anglian Old English tēman (“to give birth”) (West Saxon Old English tīeman), from Proto-West Germanic *taumijan (“to bridle”), from Proto-Germanic *taumijaną, from *taumaz ("bridle", continued in Modern English as team).

To pour (especially with rain)
To pour, as steel, from a melting pot; to fill, as a mould, with molten metal.

ety: From -teen + age. First attested in 1921.

ety: Etymology tree English teenage Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English teenager From teenage + -er.

ety: The final syllable of the numbers from thirteen to nineteen. More at teen.

ety: From the Lakota word thípi (/ˈtʰipi/), which consists of two elements: the verb thí (“to dwell”), and pi, a pluralising enclitic (a suffix-like ending that marks the subject of the verb as plural), which means they dwell. Lakota verbs can be used as nouns and this is the case with thípi, which in practice simply means house.

ety: Alteration of titter.

ety: Either from teeter + totter, or from a reduplication of either element.

Alternative form of teeter-totter.

ety: From Middle English tethen, from Old English tēþan (“to teethe”), from Proto-West Germanic *tanþijan, from Proto-Germanic *tanþijaną (“to teethe”), from Proto-Germanic *tanþs (“tooth”). Cognate with German zähnen (“to provide with teeth”).

ety: From total, the reduplicated tee acts as an intensifier, hence T-total. First use appears in 1834.

ex: I teleported home one night With Ron and Sid and Meg. Ron stole Meggie's heart away And I got Sidney's leg.

[William] Penn, therefore, exhorted the fellows not to rely on the goodness of their cause, but to submit, or at least to temporise.

s.def: To delay, especially until a more favourable time; to procrastinate.
To take temporary measures or actions to manage a situation without providing a definitive or permanent solution.

ety: From Middle English tempten, from Old French tempter (French: tenter), from Latin temptare, from tentare (“to handle, touch, try, test, tempt”), frequentative of tendere (“to stretch”). Displaced native English costning (“temptation”).

s.def: To provoke someone to do wrong, especially by promising a reward; to entice.
ex: She tempted me to eat the apple.

s.def: To attract; to allure.
ex: Its glossy skin tempted me.
The next time you are trout fishing and none of your lures tempts the fish, smoke a spoon hook and cast it.

s.def: To provoke something; to court.
ex: It would be tempting fate.

ety: From Old French temptacion, from Latin temptatio. Morphologically tempt + -ation.

s.def: The act of tempting.
The condition of being tempted.
Something attractive, tempting or seductive; an inducement, seducement, or enticement.
Pressure applied to one's thinking designed to create wrong emotions which will eventually lead to wrong actions.

ety: From Middle English tempter, temptere, temptour, temptoure, from Old French tempter, temptere, tenteor, Anglo-Norman tempteour, temptur and Middle English tempten (“to tempt”); equivalent to tempt + -er.

s.def: Someone or something that tempts, especially a man that tempts.
ex: He is a tempter of married women.

s.def: Attractive, appealing, enticing.
Seductive, alluring, inviting.
present participle and gerund of tempt
The act of subjecting somebody to temptation.

ety: Borrowed from Middle Mongol ᠲᠡᠮᠦᠵᠢᠨ (temüǰin). Possibly from Proto-Turkic *temürči(n) (“blacksmith”).

s.def: Given name of Genghis Khan.

ety: PIE word *déḱm̥ From Middle English ten, tene, from Old English tīen, from Proto-West Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Cognate with Scots ten, tene (“ten”), West Frisian tsien (“ten”), Saterland Frisian tjoon (“ten”), North Frisian tiin (“ten”). See also teen.

s.def: The number occurring after nine and before eleven, represented in Arabic numerals (base ten) as 10 and in Roman numerals as X.
ex: There is a melody upon the Earth as though ten thousand streams all sang together for their homes that they had forsaken in the hills.
A ten frame is a simple graphic tool that allows people to “see” numbers.

s.def: A set or group with ten elements.
ex: We divided the chocolates into tens to hand out to Hallowe'en visitors.
Understanding that numbers are composed of tens and ones is an important foundational concept, setting the stage for work with larger numbers.

s.def: An inexact quantity, typically understood to be between 20 and 100.
ex: Our houses are tens of meters apart, so we don't have to worry about noise from our neighbours.
tens of thousands of voters

s.def: A card in a given suit with a value of ten.
A denomination of currency, such as a banknote, with a value of ten units.
ex: Can you give me two tens for this twenty?

s.def: A perfect specimen, (particularly) a physically attractive person.
A high level of intensity.
ex: "Intensities in 10 Cities"
... Wayne Campbell (Mike Myers): "You guys kick ass. You're Double Live Gonzo. Intensities in 10 Cities. Live at Budokan."

s.def: The act of rowing ten strokes flat out.
ex: Morris gave a ten, and an unbelievable surge ran through the boat, one that I had never felt before.

ety: Calque of Biblical Hebrew עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים ('aséret had'varím, “the ten items”), from Exodus 34:28, Deuteronomy 4:13 and Deuteronomy 10:4.

s.def: A particular list of religious and moral imperatives which, according to the Old Testament of the Bible or the Hebrew Bible, were twice given or dictated by God to Moses on Mount Sinai and inscribed on two stone tablets.
A list of principal rules in a given field.
ex: These may well be the ten commandments of interpretation.
I possess the ten commandments of the hip-hop thugsta

s.def: The ten fingernails, used by women when fighting.
ex: She'd drink the gin fust and give him her ten commandments artervards, when she'd aggerawated him to try it on.
[…] once or twice, when he cut up bad, she appeared to him, and scratched his face with her ten commandments […]

s.def: The number 10,000,000.
The cardinal number 10,000.

ety: From the French tenable, from tenir (“to hold”); compare tenible.

s.def: Capable of being defended against assault or attack; defensible
ex: The island of Melos undoubtedly fell within his general conceptions of tenable empire for Athens.

s.def: capable of being maintained or justified; well-founded
ex: Back in the 1800s, many did not consider Darwin's theory of evolution to be tenable at all.

s.def: Fit for habitation, similar, or related use.
ex: Protecting or assisting occupant evacuation and safety by maintaining tenable building spaces and exit paths

ety: Borrowed from French tenace, from Spanish tenaza, from earlier tenaces, from Latin tenācēs, from teneō (“hold, grasp”).

s.def: An interrupted sequence of high cards of the same suit, such as the king and jack or the ace and queen.

ety: From Latin tenāx (“holding fast, clinging”), from tenēre (“to hold”), + -ious.

s.def: Clinging to an object or surface; adhesive.
Unwilling to yield or give up; dogged.
Holding together; cohesive.
ex: The quagmiry road, trodden into tenacious paste by the long file of human beings ahead […]

s.def: Having a good memory; retentive.

ety: From Middle French ténacité, from Latin tenācitās (whence -acity).

s.def: The quality or state of being tenacious, or persistence of purpose; tenaciousness.
ex: — Our opponents may be younger, faster and less out of shape than we are, but we have something they’ll never have! — Tenure? — Tenacity!

s.def: The quality of bodies which keeps them from parting without considerable force, as distinguished from brittleness, fragility, mobility, etc.
The effect of this attraction, cohesiveness.
The quality of bodies which makes them adhere to other bodies; adhesiveness, viscosity.

The greatest longitudinal stress a substance can bear without tearing asunder, usually expressed with reference to a unit area of the cross section of the substance, as the number of pounds per square inch, or kilograms per square centimeter, necessary to produce rupture.

ety: From French tenaille (“a pair of pincers or tongs”), from its pincer-like shape, from Latin tenāculum. See tenaculum and tenaillon.

s.def: An outwork in the main ditch of a fortification, in front of the curtain, between two bastions.

ety: From tenant + -cy.

s.def: Synonym of lease (an interest in land, its related contract or the document containing that contract); more commonly used when a lease is short-term or has a periodic rent that is not merely nominal.
ex: Most gay people know oppresion as fear of losing a job, losing a tenancy or family ties.

ety: From Middle English tenaunt, from Anglo-Norman tenaunt and Old French tenant, present participle of tenir (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre (“hold, keep”).

s.def: One who has possession of any place.
ex: c. 1782-1783, William Cowper, Joy in Martyrdom sweet tenants of this grove
the happy tenant of your shade
But not in silence pass Calypso's isles, / The sister tenants of the middle deep; [...]

s.def: One who holds a feudal tenure in real property.
law: one who holds property
One who holds a lease (a tenancy).
ex: You are just a tenant here, you say / Living in and out of this life / As cheaply as you can

s.def: Any of a number of customers serviced through the same instance of an application.
ex: multi-tenant hosting

s.def: One who owns real estate other than via allodial title.
To hold as, or be, a tenant.
To inhabit.
ex: His thin legs tenanted a pair of gambadoes fastened at the side with rusty clasps.
They lived in palatial residences[…]their harems tenanted by numerous women[…]

s.def: Misconstruction of tenet.

ety: From Middle English tenche, from Old French tenche, from Late Latin tinca.

s.def: A species of freshwater game fish, Tinca tinca.
A penitentiary.

ety: From Middle English tenden, from Middle French tendre, from Old French tendre (“to stretch, stretch out, hold forth, offer, tender”), from Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, extend, spread out”).

s.def: To make a tender of; to offer or tender.
To be likely, or probable to do something, or to have a certain habit or leaning.
ex: They tend to go out on Saturdays.
It tends to snow here in winter.
I was tending to get up later and later after the breakup.

s.def: To contribute to or toward some outcome.
ex: She had found in her everything that could tend to make a farther connection between the families undesirable.

s.def: To look after (e.g. an ill person.)
ex: We need to tend to the garden, which has become a mess.

s.def: To accompany as an assistant or protector; to care for the wants of; to look after; to watch; to guard.
ex: Shepherds tend their flocks.
There's not a sparrow or a wren, / There's not a blade of autumn grain, / Which the four seasons do not tend / And tides of life and increase lend.
Man selects only for his own good; Nature only for that of the being which she tends.

s.def: To wait (upon), as attendants or servants; to serve; to attend.
ex: Was he not companion with the riotous knights / That tend upon my father?

s.def: To await; to expect.
ex: Had I not. Four or five women once that tended me?

s.def: To be attentive to; to note carefully; to attend to.
ex: Being to descend / A ladder much in height, I did not tend / My way well down.

s.def: To manage (an anchored vessel) when the tide turns, to prevent it from entangling the cable when swinging.
To kindle; ignite; set on fire; light; inflame; burn.

ety: From Medieval Latin tendentia, from tendens, present participle of tendō.

s.def: A likelihood of behaving in a particular way or going in a particular direction; a tending toward.
ex: Denim has a tendency to fade.
I have a tendency to get bored after the first half an hour of a movie.
There's a common tendency among first-game visitors to a casino to bet overcautiously.

ex: Mao launched the struggle against the vulgar materialist tendency within the party as early as 1937.

ety: From tendency + -ious, after German tendenziös.

s.def: Having a tendency, written or spoken, with a partisan, biased or prejudiced purpose, especially a controversial one; implicitly or explicitly slanted; biased.
ex: Near-synonyms: partisan, slanted, partial, prejudiced
That he was a supporter of the cause was clear, because his reports from the front were tendentious.
It is a canard trotted out by lazy or tendentious journalists that nationalised British Railways lacked entrepreneurial flair.

ety: From Middle English tender, tendere, from Anglo-Norman tendre, Old French tendre, from Latin tener, tenerum (“soft, delicate”).

ex: Be careful: that area is tender.

ex: tender plants
tender flesh
tender fruit

s.def: Fond, loving, gentle, or sweet.
ex: Suzanne was such a tender mother to her children.
You, that are thus so tender o'er his follies, Will never do him good.
The Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.

s.def: Physically weak; not able to endure hardship.
ex: the tender and delicate woman among you

s.def: Sensible to impression and pain; easily pained.
ex: Our Bodies are not naturally more Tender than our Faces.

s.def: Young and inexperienced.
ex: I first had a girlfriend at the tender age of seven.

s.def: Adapted to excite feeling or sympathy; expressive of the softer passions; pathetic.
ex: tender expressions; tender expostulations; a tender strain
The lesser griefs that may be said, ⁠That breathe a thousand tender vows, ⁠Are but as servants in a house Where lies the master newly dead; […]

s.def: Apt to give pain; causing grief or pain; delicate.
ex: a tender subject
Things that are tender and unpleasing.

ety: From tender + foot. Refers to the delicate feet of newcomers to ranching or mining areas. First attested 1866.

s.def: An inexperienced person; a novice.
A newcomer or arriviste to the region in the American frontier (Old West and Wild West).
A Boy Scout of the lowest rank.

ety: From tender + hearted.

s.def: Compassionate for another's distress.
ex: I am tender-hearted by nature, and have found my eyes moist many a time over the scream of a wounded hare.

s.def: Easily moved to love.

ety: Borrowed from French tendon or Medieval Latin tendō, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”), modified by association with the verb tendō (“to stretch”). Compare Middle English thenoun.

ex: Kissing the tendril fingers - at first because Mina, its mother, did not - but later with a rapture begot by its breath on her breast.

duration; continuance; a state of holding on in a continuous course; general tendency; career.

an aerostat, such as a balloon, connected to the ground by a cable and winch, and used as an observation platform etc.

A tetravalent atom or radical.

A chord comprised of four notes; a tetrachord.

ety: From Ancient Greek τετράεδρον (tetráedron, “triangle-based pyramid”), from τετράεδρος (tetráedros), from τετράς (tetrás, “four”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). By surface analysis, tetra- + -hedron.

ety: From tetra- + -logy.

A combination of four symptoms.
Tetralogy of Fallot.

ety: From tetra- + -merous.

ety: From tetra- + -phobia.

s.def: Custom of avoiding the number four (4) commonly seen in those East Asian countries in whose local languages the words for "4" and "death" are paronymous or homophonous.

ety: From tetra- + -pody, from Ancient Greek τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) and πούς, ποδός (poús, podós, “foot”).

s.def: A set of four metrical feet.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).

s.def: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient Rome.
Each of the four members of a jointly ruling tetrarchy, notably of the Roman Empire since Diocletian.
An officer in charge of a fourth part of a phalanx in Ancient Greece.
Having four vascular strands in a fibrovascular cylinder or stele.

ety: From Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek τετραρχία (tetrarkhía), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”), equivalent to tetra- + -archy.

s.def: A government where power is shared by four people, especially (historical) the Herodian tetrarchy established in Judea after the death of Herod and the Tetrarchy of Diocletian which ruled the Roman Empire in the years 293-313.
ex: His imperial reorganization saw authority divided between four rulers, the Tetrarchy, to oversee the recovery.

s.def: The land ruled by such a government, either together or separately.
ex: According to Josephus, Herod Agrippa, who succeeded Antipas in his Tetrarchy, died in the seventh year of his reign;[…].
This district was included with Galilee in the tetrarchy of Herod Antipas.

ety: From Latin tetrastichon, from neuter of Ancient Greek τετράστιχον (tetrástikhon, “having four rows”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “row”).

ety: From tetra- + -style.

s.def: A building (especially a portico) that has four columns

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres Proto-Hellenic *kʷétwores Ancient Greek τέσσᾰρες (téssăres) Ancient Greek τετρᾰ- (tetră-)bor. English tetra- English syllabic English tetrasyllabic From tetra- + syllabic.

s.def: Having four syllables.

ety: Formed from tetra- (“four”) + syllable; compare Ancient Greek τετρασύλλαβος (tetrasúllabos, “of four syllables”).

s.def: A word comprising four syllables.

ety: PIE word *kʷetwóres From tetra- (prefix meaning ‘four’) + (itera)tion, from the fact that tetration is in fourth place after addition, multiplication, and exponentiation. The word was coined by the English mathematician Reuben Goodstein (1912–1985).

s.def: The arithmetic operator consisting of repeated exponentiation, by analogy with exponentiation being repeated multiplication and multiplication being repeated addition, ᵇᵃ denoting a to the power of a to the power of … to the power of a, in which a appears b times.

ety: From Middle English teter, from Old English teter, tetr, tetra, from Proto-West Germanic *tetru, from Proto-Germanic *tetruz, *tetruhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dedru-, from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to flay, split, crack”).

s.def: Any of various pustular skin conditions.
ex: heal this tetter of pedagogism that bespreads him
Angelus Politianus had a tetter in his nose continually running, fulsome in company, yet no man so eloquent and pleasing in his works.
A scabby tetter on their pelts will stick

ex: […] And all my smooth body, barked and tettered over.

s.def: Potato, or sweet potato root.

ety: Calque of German Deutschritter.

s.def: A German religious order founded in the late 12th century and known for conquering the Baltic Prussians and bringing Prussia under German control; the order exists today as a charitable organisation.

ety: Etymology tree English Texas Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English Texan From Texas + -an.

s.def: A native or inhabitant of the state of Texas, United States.
ex: In 2012, over three million Texans voted Democrat.

ety: From the practice of naming cabins after US states, the state of Texas having been recently admitted to the Union.

s.def: The topmost cabin deck on a steamboat.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Texas (also Tejas), from Hasinai Caddo táyshaʔ (“friend, ally”), used to refer to the Caddo nation.

s.def: a state of the United States of America
A state in the south-central region of the United States. Capital: Austin. Largest city: Houston.
ex: The posterists of Austin chronicled the changing social landscape and graphically redefined Texas for the rest of the country and the world […]
Approximately 100 Louisville-based KFC corporate employees will relocate to Texas over the next six months.

s.def: Several places in the United States:
A locality in the Inverell council area, north eastern New South Wales, Australia, adjacent to the Queensland town.
A rural town in southeastern Queensland, Australia, adjacent to the New South Wales locality.
The University of Texas at Austin.
A unisex given name transferred from the place name.
A former sovereign country in North America that existed from 1836 to 1846.
A surname.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-seti Proto-Indo-European *téḱseti Proto-Italic *teksō? Latin texō Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus New Latin textusbor. Old French textebor. Middle English text English text From Middle English text, from Old French texte, from Medieval Latin textus, from Latin textus (“style or texture of a work”), perfect passive participle of texō (“to weave”). Cognate to texture.

s.def: a written passage
To send a text message to; i.e. to transmit text using the Short Message Service (SMS), or a similar service, between communications devices, particularly mobile phones.
ex: Just text me when you get here.
I'll text the address to you as soon as I find it.

s.def: A writing consisting of multiple glyphs, characters, symbols or sentences.
A book, tome or other set of writings.
Anything chosen as the subject of an argument, literary composition, etc.
Ellipsis of text message, a brief written message transmitted between mobile phones.
ex: In the morning, you're vexed / He's on to the next / And you didn't even get no text

s.def: Data which can be interpreted as human-readable text.
A verse or passage of Scripture, especially one chosen as the subject of a sermon, or in proof of a doctrine.
A style of writing in large characters; also, a kind of type used in printing.
To send and receive text messages.
ex: Have you been texting all afternoon?

s.def: A program which allows a user to edit the contents of a text file, usually in an interactive way with immediate visual feedback.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see text, editor.
ex: Between 1620 and 1640 he worked as a text editor in the Patriarchal Press in Moscow.

s.def: A datafile containing only plain, human-readable text, distinct from documents with embedded formatting.
A datafile in a character encoding that allows it to be read in a nonspecialized text editor.

ety: From text + book.
