Of or pertaining to textbooks or their style, especially in being dry and pedagogical; textbooky, textbooklike.
ex: These figures are just too textbook, or papyrus-like, as if this information came off of a shelf in the Library of Alexandria

s.def: Having the typical characteristics of some class of phenomenon, so that it might be included as an example in a textbook.
ex: textbook case
It seemed too textbook, too talk-showish, but it was true.

s.def: Done exactly correctly, in an exemplary way that might be described in a textbook.
ex: Well done everyone, the tree fell exactly where we planned. That was textbook.

s.def: Learned from, or as if learned from, a textbook, as opposed to personal discovery or experience.
ex: He has a textbook understanding of company law but no practical experience of litigation.
So a lot of women will be very textbook if something meets the definition of sexual harassment, whereas a lot of men are more laissez-faire.

ety: Borrowed from Latin textile, substantive use of textilis (“woven”), from texō (“weave”).

s.def: Any material made of interlacing or matted fibres, including carpeting and geotextiles, woven or nonwoven.
ex: Near-synonym: cloth (not always differentiated)

s.def: A non-nudist.
Clothing compulsive.
ex: a textile beach

ety: From Middle English textewell, textueel, textuel, textuele, tixtuel (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin textuālis; also compare Middle French textuele; or perhaps a coinage by Chaucer from Latin textus and Middle English -el. English spelling conformed to Latin from late 15c. By surface analysis, text + -ual.

s.def: Of or pertaining to text.
ex: I see that the editor revised the document's metadata, headers, and images, but I don't see any textual changes.

s.def: Pertaining to text messages, by analogy with sexual: textual harassment, textual intercourse; compare sexting.

A person living in or coming from Thailand.
A domestic cat of a particular breed descended from cats of Thailand and somewhat resembling a Siamese.
Thai cuisine; traditional Thai food.
The main language spoken in Thailand (closely related to Lao).

ety: From Thai + -land, from Thai ไทย (tai), from ไท (tai, “Tai, or 'free' via folk etymology”).

ex: Are you from Thailand? I got you soup from Thailand!

s.def: A barangay of Banisilan, Cotabato, Philippines.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek θᾰ́λᾰμος (thắlămos)bor. Latin thalamusbor. English thalamus Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

The receptacle of a flower; a torus.
A thallus.
An inner room or nuptial chamber.

ety: From Ancient Greek θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”) (see also thalass-) and -emia (“blood”) (from αἷμα (haîma)). The etymology is suggestive of the epidemiology of the disorder, which is more common in people of Mediterranean descent. First attested in 1932.

s.def: Any of a group of inherited disorders in which the amount of hemoglobin in the blood is reduced.

ety: From French thalassique, from Ancient Greek θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”) + -ique.

pelagic

ety: From translingual Thallophyta. Surface reading of thallus + -phyte (“plant”).

s.def: Any of very many primitive plants that consist of a thallus (plant body not differentiated into roots, stems and leaves), formerly collected in the obsolete taxonomic group Thallophyta.

ety: From Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “young shoot, twig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁- (“to bloom”).

s.def: An undifferentiated plant body, such as in algae.
Any plant body lacking vascular tissue.

ety: From Middle English Temse, Temese, from Old English Temes, Temese (compare Welsh Tafwys), from Latin Tamesis, Tamesas. Variant spellings with h arose in Middle English due to the mistaken assumption of a Greek etymology. The modern spelling with a stems from either the East Saxon dialects of Middle English and Old English or the influence of Tamesis. The Latin name is from Proto-Brythonic *Tamesis, from Proto-Celtic *tamesās (“river, waters”, literally “darkness”), a masculine ā-stem of *tames,…

A town in Thames-Coromandel district, Waikato, New Zealand, situated on the Firth of Thames (a large bay) and the Coromandel Peninsula.
A surname.

ety: From Middle English than, thanne (“than; then”), from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then; when; than”), from Proto-West Germanic *þannē, an alteration of *þan (“then; than”), from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then; than”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“that”, demonstrative pronoun). Cognate with Dutch dan (“then; than”), German denn (“for; so”), German dann (“then”). Doublet of then.

s.def: Used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison.
ex: The artist worried more than was necessary: there were a lot of people at the exhibition, more than came last year.
Answer me if you can, any other way, than because the Scriptures, which are infallible, Say so.
Profits were higher than forecast.

s.def: Because; for.

Introduces a comparison, and is associated with comparatives, and with words such as more, less, and fewer. Typically, it seeks to measure the force of an adjective or similar description between two predicates.
ex: Patients diagnosed more recently are probably surviving an average of longer than two years.
No player is more skillful than Greg.

s.def: At that time; then.

The rank of a thane.

ex: Meronym: mortuary science
The work is part of a growing field called comparative thanatology — the study of how different animals react to death.

ety: Etymology tree English thanato- Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) Ancient Greek -φοβία (-phobía)der. Latin New Latinbor. English -phobia English thanatophobia From thanato- + -phobia.

s.def: A fear of death.

ety: From Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “seeing”), via the poem "Thanatopsis" by William Cullen Bryant. Although a surface analysis of thanato- + -opsis readily suggests itself and might invite a semantic expectation of deathliness, Bryant's sense of the word corresponds to "the seeing of death" rather than "the appearance/likeness of death".

s.def: Contemplation of death.

ety: From Ancient Greek Θάνατος (Thánatos).

s.def: The death drive in Freudian psychoanalysis.

ety: From Middle English theyn, thein, þein, from Old English þæġn, þeġen, þeġn, from Proto-West Germanic *þegn (“man, warrior”), from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz (“man, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- (“to give birth”); akin to Dutch degen, German Degen, Old Norse þegn and Ancient Greek τέκνον (téknon, “child”).

s.def: A rank of nobility in pre-Norman England, roughly equivalent to baron.
ex: The little island of Iona became the refuge of the sons and some thanes of Athelfrith, banished by Edwin.
Never need you fear for a single thane of your sept or nation, young warriors or old.

ety: From Middle English thank (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; attractiveness; commendation, praise; God’s grace; goodwill; merit, reward; mind, thought”), from Old English þanc, þonc (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; favour, grace; mind, thought; pleasure, satisfaction”), from Proto-Germanic *þankaz (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; mind, thought; remembrance”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to perceive; to think”). Cognates Cognate with Saterlan…

s.def: singular of thanks (“an expression of appreciation or gratitude; grateful feelings or thoughts; favour, goodwill, graciousness”)
ex: If ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.

s.def: To express appreciation or gratitude toward (someone or something).
ex: She thanked him for the lift.
I can eate no meate, I thanke you.
[S]ae laigh I need na bovv, / For, Lord be thankit, I can plough; / And vvhen I dovvna yoke a naig, / Then, Lord be thankit, I can beg; […]

s.def: In the future tense in the form one will thank someone to do something, chiefly expressing a command or criticism: to request that (someone) do something.
ex: I’ll thank you not to smoke in my house!
Our readers would not thank us for going into the badgerings which had for some time annoyed the chancellor on the subject of arrears in his court.

s.def: To express appreciation or gratitude for (something).
To respond to (someone) out of, or as if out of, appreciation or gratitude.
ex: I should summon my lord from the Queen's royal presence to do your business, should I?—I were like to be thanked with a horse-whip.

s.def: Chiefly followed by for: to credit or hold (someone or something) responsible, especially for something negative; to blame.
ex: We can thank global warming for this freak weather.

s.def: To express gratitude.

ety: Of present subjunctive mood; semantically equivalent to God be thanked.

s.def: Used to express gratitude or relief, either literally (religiously) or figuratively (nonreligiously).

ety: Form of thank God without mentioning God: thus, a secular counterpart.

s.def: Expression of relief or gratitude.

ety: From Middle English thanke yow; as with thank God, praise be to God, and praise the Lord, it was originally a present subjunctive form but is usually not parsed that way in current usage. It has also sometimes been parsed as a prodrop form of (present indicative) I thank you, a mechanism that may plausibly coexist with the other one (instances being variable).

s.def: An expression of gratitude or politeness in response to something done or given.
ex: “Thank you!” said the girl after her mom gave her a gift.
“And thank you for being so sweet,” replied her mom.
Thank ya, ma'am, thank ya, thank ya, thank ya. He's a good dog. He likes ever'body. He won' be no bother. Thank ya, ma'am, thank ya, thank ya.

s.def: Used as a polite affirmative to accept an offer.
ex: Near-synonym: please
—May I help you? —Yes, thank you.
—May I help you? —Thank you.

s.def: A polite dismissal; usually used in professional contexts.
ex: ‘No, come in,’ he said. ‘Martin, right? Have a seat.’ […] ‘Thank you, no, I won’t.’ He moved inside a little more.

s.def: Said to express greater gratitude than would be conveyed by thank you.
ex: Thank you very much indeed.

s.def: Expressing indignation that anyone could doubt the preceding statement; thanks a lot.
ex: Mr and Mrs Dursley, of number four, Privet Drive, were proud to say that they were perfectly normal, thank you very much.
Sonny came round to childsit today. (Not babysit. I’m not a baby any more – thank you very much!)
“Don’t call me honey bun,” said Mum. “I don’t need any of your Americanisms in this house, thank you very much.”

ety: From Middle English thankful, from Old English þancful, þancfull (“thoughtful, pleasing, agreeable, pleasant, thankful, grateful”), equivalent to thank + -ful. Compare Old High German undankfol (“unthankful, ungrateful”).

s.def: Obtaining or deserving thanks; thankworthy.
Showing appreciation or gratitude.
ex: I'm thankful that you helped me out today. How can I ever repay you?

ety: From Middle English thankles, equivalent to thank + -less.

s.def: Not appreciated or rewarded.
ex: One indispensable and thankless Unesco task is organizing tsunami warnings systems and pushing for tsunami education on risky shores around the world.

s.def: Ungrateful or unappreciative.

ety: From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”). More at thank.

s.def: Used to express appreciation or gratitude.
ex: Could you give me a hand, please? — Yes, sure. — Thanks. —Have you got enough now? —Yes, thanks.
Would you like some potatoes? — Thanks. —How many?

s.def: An expression of appreciation or gratitude.
ex: After all I’ve done, a simple acknowledgment is the thanks I get?

s.def: Grateful feelings or thoughts; favour, goodwill, graciousness.
plural of thank
third-person singular simple present indicative of thank

Expresses appreciation of assistance provided or services rendered by the interlocutor.

ety: From thanks + giving.

s.def: The expression of gratitude.

Only used in for thy, for-thy, which is an alternative form of forthy (“because, therefore”).

ety: From translingual Thylacinus; from Ancient Greek θύλακος (thúlakos, “pouch, sack”) + Latin -inus (-ine).

s.def: A carnivorous marsupial (†Thylacinus cynocephalus) which was native to Tasmania, now extinct.

ety: From Middle English tyme, from Old French thym, from Latin thymum, from Ancient Greek θύμον (thúmon). Displaced native Old English boþen.

s.def: Any plant of the labiate genus Thymus, such as garden thyme (Thymus vulgaris), a warm, pungent aromatic, that is much used to give a relish to seasoning and soups.

ety: From thymus + -ine. Thymine was first isolated in 1893 by Albrecht Kossel and Albert Neumann from calves' thymus glands, hence its name.

s.def: A heterocyclic base, 5-methylpyrimidine-2,4(1H,3H)-dione; it pairs with adenine in DNA.

ety: From New Latin thymus, from Ancient Greek θύμος (thúmos, “warty excrescence, (also, as used by Galen) thymus gland”).

s.def: Ellipsis of thymus gland (“A ductless gland, consisting mainly of lymphatic tissue, located behind the top of the breastbone. It is most active during puberty, after which it shrinks in size. It plays an important role in the development of the immune system and produces lymphocytes.”).
ex: For a very long time the role of the thymus in the body was a complete mystery.

Of, relating to, or being the thyroid gland.

Ellipsis of thyroid cartilage.
Ellipsis of thyroid gland.
The largest cartilage in the larynx; the Adam’s apple

ety: From New Latin glandula thyreoidea, coined by Thomas Wharton in 1656.

s.def: A large butterfly-shaped endocrine gland situated on the front of the neck that produces various hormones.

s.def: A thyroid hormone, with the chemical formula C₁₅H₁₁I₄NO₄, that regulates cell metabolism and growth.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrse, torse, and torso.

s.def: A staff topped with a conical ornament, carried by Bacchus or his followers.
ex: 1882, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, The Poet's Calendar In my hand I bear / The thyrsus, tipped with fragrant cones of pine.
As good to grow on graves / As twist about a thyrsus.
The champagne was done, and she upturned the bottle to hold it like a thyrsus.

s.def: A species of inflorescence; a dense panicle, as in the lilac and horse-chestnut.

ety: From Middle English thy-selfe, thiself, thi-zelf, equivalent to thy + -self. Compare Middle English thou-self.

s.def: yourself (as the object of a verb or preposition or as an intensifier); reflexive case of thou
ex: Physician, heal thyself.

ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanisation of Mandarin 天山 (Tiān Shān), from Uyghur تەڭرىتاغ (tengritagh, literally “Mountains of God (Tengri)”) (Tengri Tagh).

s.def: A mountain range in Central Asia.
ex: The excavation of the KaraDjigach site, in the Chu-Valley within the foothills of the Tian Shan mountains of Kyrgyzstan, in August 1886.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

s.def: The three-tiered papal crown.
An ornamental coronet.
ex: [T]heir tiaræ are like those of the magi; […]
The Bactrians wore tiaræ like the Persians, with bamboo bows, and short javelins.
For the latter bears a pair of winged bulls with tiaræ and feathered necks, after the so much admired Assyrian prototype; […]

s.def: To adorn as a tiara.
ex: Brilliants tiaraed her head.
A parure of brilliants tiaraed her dark head.
Averting his eyes he glanced hastily at his cards; a jeweled tracery of sweat tiaraed his forhead.^([sic])

s.def: To adorn with a tiara.
ex: He tiaraed her head.
I see how this Semiramis, imitating a man, has tiaraed her head and cleverly captivates the eyes of those standing about; […]

ety: From Latin Tiberias, from Ancient Greek Τιβεριάς (Tiberiás), after the Emperor Tiberius.

s.def: A town in the Northern District, on the Sea of Galilee in Israel.
A locality in Southern Midlands council area, eastern Tasmania, Australia.

ety: From Latin Tiberius, literally 'Of the Tiber', from Tiberis, the river Tiber. Also note Faliscan equivalent *Tiferios. The name is mistaken by some to be of Etruscan origin but note the borrowed variants, Thefarie (from Faliscan) and Teperi (from Latin).

s.def: given name
A male given name from Latin of mostly historical use; a specific person so named.
ex: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee,

ety: From the place name Tibet.

s.def: A woolen fabric generally printed in colours; a heavy fabric used for the same purposes as furs, made of goat hair, black and finely curled.
ex: The chief demand in men's-wear fabrics is for combed and milled fabrics such as worsteds, kerseys, tibets, meltons, etc.

ety: Etymology tree English Tibet Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Old French -ainder. Middle English -an English -an English Tibetan From Tibet + -an.

s.def: Pertaining to Tibet, the Tibetan people, culture, or language.
ex: After many years, Buddhism touched every aspect of Tibetan life, including how to treat the earth and plants and animals.

s.def: a person
A native of Tibet
A language of Tibet
A large dog of a breed from Central Asia, having a medium to long double coat in a wide variety of colors, sometimes with white markings around neck, chest, and legs.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tībia (“shin bone, leg”).

s.def: The inner and usually the larger of the two bones of the leg or hind limb below the knee, the shinbone.
The second segment from the end of an insect's leg, between the femur and tarsus.
The third segment from the end of an arachnid's leg, between the patella and metatarsus.
A musical instrument of the flute kind, originally made of the leg bone of an animal.

ety: Imitative; from tick-tack, used earlier to denote games in which the pieces made clicking sounds.

s.def: A game in which two players take turns placing circles and crosses on a 3x3 grid and attempt to obtain three of the same symbols in a straight line.

ety: From Middle English tyke, teke, from Old English ticia (“parasitic animal, tick”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīkō, compare Dutch teek, German Zecke.

s.def: A tiny woodland arachnid of the suborder Ixodida.
A relatively quiet but sharp sound generally made repeatedly by moving machinery.
ex: The steady tick of the clock provided a comforting background for the conversation.

s.def: A mark on any scale of measurement; a unit of measurement.
ex: At midday, the long bond is up a tick.

s.def: A jiffy (unit of time defined by basic timer frequency).
A short period of time, particularly a second.
ex: I'll be back in a tick.

s.def: A periodic increment of damage or healing caused by an ongoing status effect.
Each of the fixed time periods, in a tick-based game, in which players or characters may perform a set number of actions.
A mark (✓) made to indicate agreement, correctness, or acknowledgement.
ex: Indicate that you are willing to receive marketing material by putting a tick in the box

s.def: A bird seen (or heard) by a birdwatcher, for the first time that day, year, trip, etc., and thus added to a list of observed birds.
ex: There are few birders who have not had stringy ticks on their lists at some stage.

s.def: A whinchat (Saxicola rubetra).

ety: * tick + bite

s.def: A bite from a tick that can pass various illnesses to the bitten host.
any of various diseases transmitted by ticks
To sign an item on a list with a tick mark, especially as a signal that the item has been verified or completed.
ex: I ticked off Harry today because he announced he was present.
I ticked three things off the list in my head, and had only four chores left to do.

s.def: To list (create or recite a list).
ex: In a lengthy missive dispatched the next afternoon, Wheeler ticked off a laundry list of reasons why he could not obey Bragg's order.

s.def: To annoy, aggravate.
ex: It really ticks me off when people don't use proper punctuation.

s.def: To reprimand.
ex: Fred was ticked off by the teacher for playing around in class.

s.def: A viral infectious disease of the central nervous system borne by ticks, which most often manifests as meningitis, encephalitis, or meningoencephalitis.

ety: Imitative. See tick.

s.def: The sound of the ticking of an analog clock.
Time is running out; a deadline is approaching.
ex: Near-synonym: clock is ticking
You may be smart enough to elude the law for five years, but your time has run out. Tick tock, motherfucker.

s.def: Alternative spelling of tic bean

ety: From tick + -er.

s.def: One who makes a tick mark.
A watch (timepiece).
ex: A right nice ticker it was. Real gold.

s.def: A birdwatcher who aims to see (and tick off on a list) as many bird species as possible.
A beer drinker who aims to try as many different beers as possible and keeps a record of all the beers they have drunk.
ex: My weekday visit found a great mix of luncheoners, locals and real ale tickers.
This book has not been written with the goal of pleasing beer geeks, tickers, fetishists, raters or advocates.
Today's tickers are equipped with smartphones with downloaded apps like Untappd. I've seen tickers peruse beer lists for new beers they haven't tried.

s.def: A measuring or reporting device, particularly one which makes a ticking sound as the measured events occur.
ex: The ticker was showing an increased rate of flow.

s.def: A ticker tape, either the traditional paper kind or a scrolling message on a screen.
ex: I checked the prices on the ticker one last time before placing the trade.
To my surprise, the ticker showed that the deal had already gone through.

s.def: A heart, especially a human one.
ex: My ticker gave out and I had to go to the hospital for surgery.

ety: Borrowed from Middle Scots tikkat, tikket, from Middle French etiquet m, estiquet m, and etiquette f, estiquette f (“a bill, note, label, ticket”), from Old French estechier, estichier, estequier (“to attach, stick”), (compare Picard estiquier (“to stick, pierce”)), from Frankish *stikkjan, *stekan (“to stick, pierce, sting”), from Proto-Germanic *stikaną, *stikōną, *staikijaną (“to be sharp, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab”). Doublet of etiquette. Mor…

s.def: A small document that acts as proof of something, often thereby granting the holder some ability.
ex: I've got two tickets for the match on Saturday; want to come?

s.def: A service request, used to track complaints or requests that an issue be handled.
A citation for a traffic violation.
A list of candidates for an election, or a particular theme to a candidate's manifesto.
ex: Joe has joined the party's ticket for the county elections.
Joe will be running on an anti-crime ticket.

s.def: A small note or notice.
ex: He constantly read his lectures twice a week for above forty years, giving notice of the time to his auditors in a ticket on the school doors.
Under each coin was a circular ticket with written particulars of the specimen accompanying it.

s.def: A tradesman's bill or account (hence the phrase on ticket and eventually on tick).
ex: Your courtier is mad to take up silks and velvets / On ticket for his mistress.

s.def: A label affixed to goods to show their price or description.
A visiting card.
ex: I asked for a card, please, and she was quite put about, and said that she didn't require tickets to get in where she visited.
"Mr. Gibbs come in just now," said Mrs. Blewett, "and left his ticket over the chimley. There 'tis. I haven't touched it."

s.def: A warrant.
ex: […] I need a ticket, Bobby.” Agnor knew a ticket meant a search warrant.

s.def: To issue someone a ticket, as for travel or for a violation of a local or traffic law.
A person who checks that passengers on public transport (such as trains or buses) have valid tickets for their journey and, in some systems, to mark or scan those tickets so they cannot be reused.
A machine that prints tickets automatically after the customer determines the destination and pays for it.
An office or booth where tickets may be purchased to allow admittance or for travel.

ety: From tick (“sheet, cover”) + -ing (“material, collection”).

s.def: A strong cotton or linen fabric used to cover pillows and mattresses.
ex: Harvey saw with disgust that there were no sheets on his bed-place. He was lying on a piece of dingy ticking full of lumps and nubbles.

s.def: A sound of something that ticks. (For example, the second hand on a clock face.)
ex: Were they indeed the tickings of a hundred clocks — the fine low inward breathings of Time's children!

s.def: An illusional style of dance where one moves his or her body to the "tic" of the music creating a strobe or animated effect.
present participle and gerund of tick
ex: a ticking time bomb

s.def: A marking that occurs on some horses, involving white flecks of hair at the flank, and white hairs at the base of the tail, called a skunk tail or rabicano, sometimes referred to as birdcatcher ticks.

ety: From Middle English tiklen, tikelen, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a frequentative form of Middle English tikken (“to touch lightly”), thus equivalent to tick + -le; or perhaps related to Old English tinclian (“to tickle”). Compare North Frisian tigele (“to tickle”) (Hallig dialect), and tiikle (“to tickle”) (Amrum dialect), German dialectal zicklen (“to excite; stir up”). Alternatively, from a metathetic alteration of Middle English kitelen ("to tickle"; see kittle). Both are ultimately so…

s.def: To touch repeatedly or stroke delicately in a manner which typically causes laughter, pleasure and twitching.
ex: He tickled Nancy's tummy, and she started to giggle.
If you tickle us, do we not laugh?

s.def: To feel as if the body part in question is being tickled.
ex: My nose tickles, and I'm going to sneeze!

s.def: The act of tickling.
An itchy feeling resembling the result of tickling.
ex: I have a persistent tickle in my throat.

s.def: A light tap of the ball.
ex: There's a very fine line between a tickle and an edge!

s.def: A narrow strait, such as between an island and the shore.
ex: Cow Head itself is a prominent headland connected to the settlement by a natural causeway, or ‘tickle’ as the Newfoundlanders prefer it.

s.def: To appeal to someone's taste, curiosity etc.
To cause delight or amusement in.
ex: He was tickled to receive such a wonderful gift.
Behold the child, by Nature's kindly law, Pleas'd with a rattle, tickled with a straw.
Such a nature Tickled with good success, disdains the shadow Which he treads on at noon.

s.def: To feel titillation.
ex: He with secret joy therefore Did tickle inwardly in every vein.

s.def: To catch fish in the hand (usually in rivers or smaller streams) by manually stimulating the fins.

ety: From tickle + -er.

s.def: One who tickles.
A person who or thing which amuses or excites.
A reminder.
ex: Put it in the tickler file for next week.

s.def: A latex condom that has additional protrusions, for enhancing the sexual pleasure of the user.
Something puzzling or difficult; a conundrum.
A tickler file, file cabinet, or similar containing memoranda of deadlines arranged in date order.
A prong used by coopers to extract bungs from casks.
A dram of spirits.
Something puzzling; a poser.
A small notebook that fits the pocket or pocket notebook.

ety: Etymology tree English tickle Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -isch English -ish English ticklish From tickle + -ish.

s.def: Sensitive or susceptible to being tickled.
ex: She is ticklish only on her tummy and the bottoms of her feet.

s.def: Touchy, sensitive, or delicate.
ex: Opening round three, Enderby moved the ticklish issue of whether to advise the Hong Kong government of the intelligence regarding Ko.

s.def: A kind of backgammon played with both men and pegs.
ex: And that those pretended Tumults were chastiz'd by thir own Army for new Tumults, is not prov'd by a Game at Tictack with words

s.def: Dated form of tick tock.
A repeated ticking noise like that made by a clock or a watch.
To make that kind of noise.
To play a prank that involves making noise outside a person's house by various means.
Alternative spelling of tic-tac-toe.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis Proto-Germanic *tīdiz Proto-West Germanic *tīdi Old English tīd Middle English tyde English tide Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English tidal From tide + -al. Probably a hybrid forma…

s.def: Relating to tides.
The locking of the rotation of a satellite (moon or planet) to its orbit, such that one side always faces the body around which it is orbiting.
A large and sudden rise and fall in the tide.
A large, sudden, and disastrous wave of water caused by a tremendous disturbance in the ocean; a tsunami. (See Usage notes below.)
ex: The last tidal wave here killed twenty and left thousands homeless.

s.def: A large, sudden inundation of water from the storm surge, or waves of that surge; a sudden surge of river water.
A sudden and powerful surge.
ex: As the doors opened, a tidal wave of people flooded into the room.
I was overcome by a tidal wave of emotions.
But this is no stream, folks. This will be a tidal wave that can swamp our democracy.

s.def: A crest of ocean water; a wave.
A crest of ocean water resulting from tidal forces.
Having undergone tidal locking.
ex: Kruban is a tidally-locked Venusian hothouse, its surface perpetually obscured by clouds of sulfur and carbon dioxides.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis Proto-Germanic *tīdiz Proto-West Germanic *tīdi Old English tid English bit English tidbit From Old English tid (“fond, tender, nice”) + English bit (“morsel”).

s.def: A part of poultry when prepared as food
A tasty morsel (of food).
A short item of news, gossip, or information.
ex: Maya: Maybe we should leave a juicy tidbit for someone to read!

s.def: Generically, any small thing.
ex: This little book is very entertaining—quite a literary tidbit.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis Proto-Germanic *tīdiz Proto-West Germanic *tīdi Old English tīd Middle English tyde English tide Inherited from Middle English tyde, from Old English tīd, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis. Related to time. Cognate with Dutch tijd (“time”), German Zeit (“time”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, N…

s.def: A point or period of time identified or described by a qualifier.
ex: Eventide, noontide, morrowtide, nighttide, moontide, harvesttide, wintertide, summertide, springtide, autumntide etc.

s.def: The daily fluctuation in the level of the sea caused by the gravitational influence of the moon and the sun.
ex: The Bristol Channel has some of the world's largest tides.

s.def: The associated flow of water.
ex: A lot of driftwood was brought in on the tide.
We can cross to the island when the tide is out, but it won't move out until around five o'clock.

s.def: Any similar gravitational effect on Earth or other body.
ex: As well as sea tides, there are much smaller land tides.
By far the largest tides on Europa are those caused by the gravitational attraction of Jupiter.

s.def: A high-volume flow, literal or figurative; a current or flood.
ex: The sewer burst, and a tide of sewage poured into nearby properties.
A tide of people crossed over the border.
We've encountered a tide of problems.

s.def: The tendency or direction of causes, influences, or events; course; current.
ex: The tide of public opinion has turned.
There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune […]
This is the crap our children are learning / But oh, oh, oh, the tide is turning

s.def: Time, notably anniversary, period or season linked to an ecclesiastical feast.
ex: [...] and rest their weary limbs a tide.
Which, at th'appointed tyde, / Each one did make his Bryde
at the tide / Of Christ his birth

s.def: A time.
ex: The doctor's no good this tide.

s.def: The period of twelve hours.
To cause to float with the tide; to drive or carry with the tide or stream.
ex: They are tided down the stream.

der: a rising tide lifts all boats

ety: From tide + land.

s.def: The area at the shore that is exposed to the effects of the tide.
Synonym of riptide.

ety: From tide + water.

s.def: Water affected by the flow of the tide, especially tidal streams.
The seaboard.
ex: She was born Mary Blair Rice, the daughter of a prominent tidewater Virginia family whose roots stretched back to the colonial era.

s.def: A structure or house with large wraparound porches and hip roofs designed for wet and hot climates.

ety: From tide + way.

s.def: A channel in which the tide sets, especially in the tidal part of a river.
ex: Quite near could also be seen several ancient wooden warships, and always a variety of craft slipping up and down the tideway.

ety: From a merger of Middle English tiding, tidinge, from Late Old English tīdung, with Middle English tidinde, tidende, from or influenced by Old Norse tíðindi (“news, tidings”), both connected to Old English tīdan (“to befall; happen”). Though it is sometimes assumed that the form in -ind/-end is original and later assimilated to -ing, the cognates Dutch tijding and German Zeitung point to inheritance from Proto-West Germanic *tīdungō. By surface analysis, tide (“time”) + -ing.

s.def: News; new information.
ex: But yet it is pity we had lost tidings of our souls: actually we shall have to go in quest of them again, or worse in all ways will befall!
Glad tidings we bring / To you and your kin.
(I am indebted to the prolific substacker Noah Smith for this list of happy tidings.)

s.def: plural of tiding; news
ex: When we were gone astray / O tidings of comfort and joy
Glad tidings we bring / To you and your kin.

ety: From Middle English tidy, tydy, tidi (“timely, seasonal, opportune”), from tide (“time”) + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian tiedig (“timely, early”), Dutch tijdig (“timely”), German Low German tiedig (“timely”), German zeitig (“seasonal, timely”), Danish tidig (“timely”), Swedish tidig (“timely”).

s.def: Arranged neatly and in order.
ex: She always kept her desk immaculately tidy; nothing was ever out of place.

s.def: Not messy; neat and controlled.
ex: Keep Britain tidy by picking up litter.

s.def: Satisfactory; comfortable.
Generous, considerable.
ex: The scheme made a tidy profit.
Two hundred thousand people! Miss Glory, that's a tidy lot. Not bad.

s.def: In good time; at the right time; timely; seasonable; opportune; favourable; fit; suitable.
ex: if weather be fair and tidy

s.def: Brave; smart; skillful; fine; good.
Appropriate or suitable as regards occasion, circumstances, arrangement, or order.
Normalized in a certain way that optimizes for data analysis.
To make tidy; to neaten.
A container or other device for storing or organizing loose items in a tidy fashion.
ex: desk tidy; sink tidy; cable tidy
It was in the days when[…]every scrap of cotton or linen found its way into the ‘tidy’.

ety: From Middle English teye (“cord, chain”), from Old English tēag, tēah (“cord, chain”), from Proto-West Germanic *taugu, from Proto-Germanic *taugō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-. Compare Danish tov, Icelandic taug.

s.def: To attach or fasten (one thing to another) by string or the like.
ex: Tie him to the tree.
In bond of virtuous love together tied.

s.def: A knot; a fastening.
A knot of hair, as at the back of a wig.
A necktie (item of clothing consisting of a strip of cloth tied around the neck). See also bow tie, black tie.
A twist tie, a piece of wire embedded in paper, strip of plastic with ratchets, or similar object which is wound around something and tightened.
A lace-up shoe.
ex: Oxford ties; Derby ties
[…] the tip of her russet boot almost grazed that of his Oxford tie.

s.def: A structural member firmly holding two pieces together.
ex: Ties work to maintain structural integrity in windstorms and earthquakes.

s.def: A horizontal wooden or concrete structural member that supports and ties together rails.
The situation in which two or more participants in a competition are placed equally.
ex: It's two outs in the bottom of the ninth, tie score.

s.def: A connection between people or groups of people, especially a strong connection.
ex: the sacred ties of friendship or of duty
the ties of allegiance; the ties that bind
Occasions that reinforce the ties of kindred.

s.def: A rope, strap, chain, or line used to secure and hold down a load, cargo, equipment during transport.

Of an action: that may be brought in any county
ex: in transitory actions, for injuries that might have happened anywhere

ety: From Middle English translaten (“to transport, translate, transform”), from Anglo-Norman translater, from Latin trānslātus, perfect passive participle of trānsferō (“to transport, carry across, translate”). See also -ate (verb-forming suffix). Distant doublet of transfer, see collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others. In this sense, displaced Old English wendan (“to translate,” also the word for “to turn” and “to change”).

s.def: Senses relating to the change of information, etc., from one form to another.
ex: Hans translated my novel into Welsh.

s.def: Senses relating to a change of position.
ex: After translating this plane, parallel to the ground line, to the position n#95;1L#95;1r#95;1, these points appear at n#95;1 and r#95;1.

s.def: To entrance (“place in a trance”), to cause to lose recollection or sense.
ex: William was translated by the blow to the head he received, being unable to speak for the next few minutes.

s.def: To repair (used shoes, boots or other clothing) for resale.
In Euclidean spaces: a set of points obtained by adding a given fixed vector to each point of a given set.
ex: [F]ractions with a defining relation are nothing but linear orthogonal arrays or their translates.

ety: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”). Equivalent to translate + -ion. Displaced native Old English wending.

s.def: The product or end result of an act of translating, in its various senses.
act of translating between languages
The act of translating, in its various senses:
ex: This old text needs translation into modern English before it is published.

s.def: A multilingual dictionary assisting translation between two or more languages.
ex: Wiktionary is meant to be both an explanatory dictionary and a translation dictionary.

ety: Coined by American poet, translator and translation scholar James S. Holmes in 1972 in his paper “The name and nature of translation studies”.

s.def: The study of the theory and practice of translating and interpreting, especially in an academic context, combining elements of social science and the humanities.

ety: Directly from Latin trānslātor and French translator, and also from Middle English translatour, from Old French translatour, translateur, etc., from Latin trānslātor, from trānslātus (“carried across”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from trānsferō (“carry across”), from trans (“across”) + ferō (“bear, carry”), q.v. Equivalent to translate + -or.

s.def: someone or something that translates meaning from one language to another
A person or thing that translates meaning from one language into another, particularly
ex: Mr. C. Blair Leighton... lithographer... was one of the earliest translators of water and oil pictures by the chromatic process.

s.def: Synonym of carrier, a person who transports something, now particularly (Roman Catholicism, rare) holy relics.
Synonym of repairer, particularly of leather or cloth goods.
A used and repaired shoe, boot, or other item of clothing.
Synonym of repeater, a thing that automatically retransmits an incoming message along a telegraph line.
A thing that converts energy from one form to another.
The retinaculum of asclepiads.

ety: From trans- (“across”) + lingual (“having to do with languages or tongues”).

s.def: Existing in multiple languages.
ex: The nose's comic potency is enhanced by the Indo-European rootedness of its own name, securing it a pivotal role in translingual games.
You must establish that a translingual approach is rhetorically justified, critically relevant, and communicates ideas with clarity.

s.def: Having the same meaning in many languages.
ex: No is the translingual symbol for the chemistry element nobelium.

s.def: Containing words of multiple languages.
ex: Darien can make translingual jokes

s.def: Operating between different languages.
Occurring or being measured across the tongue.
ex: Simultaneous recordings of the translingual potential and integrated neural response of the rat.

To pass into another body after death.

ety: Borrowed from Latin trānsmigrātiō.

A change from one state of existence to another.
The movement of a soul from one body to another after death.

ety: Borrowed from Latin transmissionem (accusative of transmissio), from transmittere.

The fact of being transmitted.
Something that is transmitted, such as a message, picture, or a disease; the sending of such a thing.
The passage of a nerve impulse across synapses.
A device, usually an assembly of gears (gearbox) plus a clutch or torque converter, through which power is sent from the engine to the driveshaft in an automobile (motor car or motor truck).

The right possessed by an heir or legatee of transmitting to his successor(s) any inheritance, legacy, right, or privilege, to which he is entitled, even if he should die without enjoying or exercising it.
The passing of a pathogen or communicable disease from an infected host individual or group to a conspecific individual or group.
The passing down of a text through time.

The mathematical function of an electromagnetic wave is a measure of the change undergone by the amplitude of the wave as it propagates in a given direction, which is also called the propagation constant.

ety: From Middle English transmitten, borrowed from Latin trānsmittō (“transmit”, verb, literally “across-send”).

s.def: To send or convey from one person, place or thing to another.
To spread or pass on (something such as a disease or a signal).
To impart, convey or hand down by inheritance or heredity.
To convey or conduct (energy or force) through a mechanism or medium.
ex: The tractive and braking forces are transmitted to the body through a downward projecting pivot pin in the normal way.

s.def: To send out (a signal, as opposed to receive).
ex: A Mayday call was transmitted by the stricken vessel.

s.def: To go out; to be sent, conveyed, spread, passed on, or communicated.
ex: The Mayday call transmitted successfully.

s.def: To communicate (news or information, especially electronically).

ety: 17th century; origin uncertain, but possibly from transmigure, transmigrate. It is also possible that this word is a formation derived from maugre, hence it originally signified the "evil eye", but under the influence of the former etymologies shifted its meaning to its sense of "transformation". Another possibility is a humorous blending of transfigure and modify.

s.def: To substantially or completely alter the form of.
ex: Our present Governors (who have transmografide Monarchy into a Free State) ...

Openness; accessibility to scrutiny.

Obvious; readily apparent; easy to see or understand.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French transpirer, from Medieval Latin transpirare (“to breathe through”), from Latin trans (“across”) spirare (“to breathe”). Anything that is transplanted, especially and archetypically a plant.

English triage Borrowed from French triage, from trier (“to sort”).

s.def: The process of sorting patients so as to determine the order in which they will be treated (for example, by assigning precedence according to the urgency of illness or injury).
Assessment or sorting according to quality, need, etc., especially to determine how resources will be allocated.
ex: [Mike Davis] notes that the 'late capitalist triage of humanity' has 'already taken place'.

s.def: A facility within a hospital that screens walk-in patients and determines which department or clinic to send them to. (See also triage center.)
ex: I knew where most of the medical supplies were kept. I went to triage. The room was chaos.
Triage was busy and noisy, and suddenly I had no energy.
She was told to hydrate and try some Tylenol and if it got worse, she was recommended to go to triage for evaluation.

s.def: The process of prioritizing bugs to be fixed.
That which is picked out, especially broken coffee beans.
A marshalling yard, classification yard.

ety: Etymology tree Old French trier Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -al Anglo-Norman trialubor. Middle English trial English trial From Middle English trial, triall, from Anglo-Norman trial, triel, from trier (“to pick out, cull”) + -al. More at English try.

s.def: A meeting or series of meetings in a court of law at which evidence is presented to a judge (and sometimes a jury) to allow them to decide on a legal matter (especially whether an accused person is guilty of a crime).
ex: If you are convicted at trial, you have the right to file an appeal.
He was charged with war crimes and brought to trial before the International Tribunal.
The journalists have been held in custody for three years without trial.

s.def: A difficult or annoying experience or person; (especially religion) such an experience seen as a test of faith and piety.
ex: That boy was a trial to his parents.
That they are Cowards, many have said, but few have found it so in the time of Trial.
Poor Justine was very ill; but other trials were reserved for her.

s.def: chance to test something out
An occasion on which a person or thing is tested to find out how well they perform or how suitable they are.
ex: Jama saw the sweaty, smelly work as a kind of test that, if passed, would entitle him to see his father, a trial of his worth as a son and as a man.

s.def: The action of trying (to do) something, especially more than once. (This sense is still current in the expression trial and error.)
ex: Finding my first Seed did not grow, which I easily imagin’d was by the Drought, I sought for a moister Piece of Ground to make another Trial in,
He summoned up all his strength for one last trial, and bent his faltering steps towards [the house].
After a dozen trials he succeeded in lighting the lantern,

s.def: Pertaining to a trial or test.
Attempted on a provisional or experimental basis.
To carry out a series of tests on (a new product, procedure etc.) before marketing or implementing it.
ex: The warning system was extensively trialed before being fitted to all our vehicles.
In Britain, bots are being trialed to bridge waiting times for people seeking therapy but unable to get appointments and as an e-triage tool.

s.def: To try out (a new player) in a sports team.
ex: The team trialled a new young goalkeeper in Saturday's match, with mixed results.

s.def: Characterized by having three (usually equivalent) components.
The process of finding a solution to a problem by trying many possible solutions and learning from mistakes until success is attained.
ex: Navigating by trial and error may get you there eventually, but using a map is faster.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English triangle, from Old French triangle, from Latin triangulum, noun use of adjective triangulus (“three-cornered, having three angles”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“corner, angle”), equivalent to tri- + -angle.

s.def: A polygon with three sides and three angles.
ex: Meronyms: angle, side, cathetus, leg, hypotenuse; see also Thesaurus:polygon
The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.

s.def: The structure of systems composed with three interrelated objects.
A draughtsman's square in the form of a right-angled triangle.
A frame formed of three poles stuck in the ground and united at the top, to which people were bound for corporal punishment.
ex: I was flogged in 1840. To this day I feel a pain in the chest from the triangles.

s.def: Any of various large papilionid butterflies of the genus Graphium.
A triangular formation of railway tracks, with a curve on at least one side.
ex: After turning on the triangle at Jeumont, we set off light engine back to Aulnoye.

s.def: A set square.
A percussion instrument made by forming a metal rod into a triangular shape which is open at one angle. It is suspended from a string and hit with a metal bar to make a resonant sound.
A triangular piece of equipment used for gathering the balls into the formation required by the game being played.
A love triangle.
ex: One of the writers' most pleasing inventions was to treat the triangle love story as comedy.

ety: From Middle English triangulare, trianguler, triangulere, from Old French triangulaire, triangulier and Latin triangulāris. By surface analysis, tri- + -angular.

s.def: Shaped like a triangle.
Of, or pertaining to, triangles.
Having a triangle as a base; as, a triangular prism, a triangular pyramid.
Having three elements or parties; trilateral, tripartite.
A prism with a triangular base.

ety: From Latin triangulum + -ate or Medieval Latin *triangulāt-, the past participial stem of *triangulō. Compare French trianguler.

s.def: To locate by means of triangulation.
ex: "I'll give you a check now," I said abruptly, and saw Selina's green eyes triangulate angrily on my face.

s.def: To pit two others against each other in order to achieve a desired outcome or to gain an advantage; to "play both sides against the middle".
To divide into triangles.
Synonym of triangular.

ety: From Medieval Latin triangulātiō (“triangulation”), from triangulō (“to triangulate”) + -tiō (noun-forming suffix). Triangulō is derived from triangulus (“triangular; triangle”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“angle; corner”). By surface analysis, triangulate + ion; cognate with French triangulation.

s.def: A technique in which distances and directions are estimated from an accurately measured baseline and the principles of trigonometry; (countable) an instance of the use of this technique.
The network of triangles so obtained, that are the basis of a chart or map.
A delaying move in which the king moves in a triangular path to force the advance of a pawn.
A subdivision of a planar object into triangles, and by extension the subdivision of a higher-dimension geometric object into simplices.
A process by which an unknown location is found using three known distances from known locations.
The practice of repositioning one's group or oneself on the political spectrum in an attempt to capture the centre.
The use of three (or more) researchers to interview the same people or to evaluate the same evidence to reduce the impact of individual bias.

ety: From Trias (“three-layered geologic strata between the Permian and Jurassic”) < German Trias < Ancient Greek τριάς (triás, “triad”), + -ic. Coined in 1841 by geologist Friedrich August von Alberti (1795–1878).

s.def: A geologic period within the Mesozoic era, comprising lower, middle and upper epochs from about 250 to 200 million years ago.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English tribe, tribu, from Old French tribu, from Latin tribus. Doublet of tribus. Displaced native Old English hād (“tribe, group”).

s.def: A socially cohesive group of people within a society.
ex: Near-synonyms: nation; ingroup
She found her tribe among fellow cross-stitchers.

s.def: An ethnic group larger than a band or clan (and which may contain clans) but smaller than a nation (and which in turn may constitute a nation with other tribes). The tribe is often the basis of ethnic identity.
ex: the Twelve Tribes of Israel; Germanic tribes; Celtic tribes
The Formation of Kazakh Identity: From Tribe to Nation-state

s.def: A tribal nation or people.
ex: This leaves for consideration of this group of small tribes, or subtribes, so far as mapped by the writer quoted, the Teule, Cazcan, and Tecuexe.

s.def: A nation or people considered culturally primitive, as may be the case in Africa, Australia or Native America.
A class or group of things.
A group of apes who live and work together.
A hierarchical rank between family and genus.
ex: This family includes the whole of the wellknown tribe of Pigeons and Doves.
Almost all the tribe of antelopes are of a gentle and social nature.

s.def: A species or group of similar species of animal.
ex: The cod may not improperly be placed at the head of the migrating or wandering tribe of fish.

s.def: A group of affiliated Mardi Gras Indians.
A collective noun for various animals.

ety: From tribo- + -logy.

s.def: The science and engineering of interacting surfaces in relative motion; the study and application of technology using the principles of friction, lubrication and wear.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From the Latin tribrachys, from the Ancient Greek τρῐ́βρᾰχῠς (trĭ́brăkhŭs), from τρῐ- (trĭ-, “tri-”) + βρᾰχῠ́ς (brăkhŭ́s, “short”). Compare the French tribraque.

s.def: A metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.
ex: For your foote tribracchus of all three short, ye haue very few trissillables.
We may vse a Spondee or Iambick and sometime a Tribrack or Dactile.
The plain tribrach is frequent in every one’s reading.

s.def: A figure or object having three arms or branches.
ex: An optical plummet, built into either the tribrach or alidade of total station instruments, permits accurate centering over a point.

ety: From Middle English tribulation, from Old French tribulacion, from Late Latin trībulātiō (“distress, trouble, tribulation, affliction”), from Latin tribulāre (“to press, probably also thresh out grain”), from trībulum (“a sledge consisting of a wooden block studded with sharp pieces of flint or with iron teeth, used for threshing grain”), from terēre (“to rub”); see trite.

s.def: Any adversity; a trying period or event.
ex: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer
Baltimore's tribulations were indeed sore; there was no peace for him day nor night.
Essentially stoic, passive characters, Kristina and the others triumph by surviving — by outliving their plagues and tribulations.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Old French tribunal, from Latin tribūnal (“tribunal”), from tribus (“tribe”).

s.def: An assembly including one or more judges to conduct judicial business; a court of law.
A kind of village hall used to transact business, to quarter troops and travellers, and to confine prisoners.

ety: From Middle English tribune, from Old French tribun, tribune, from Latin tribunus (“tribune, tribal leader”), from tribus (“tribe”).

s.def: An elected official in Ancient Rome, a tribune of the plebs.
A military officer in Ancient Rome ranking below a legate and above a centurion, a military tribune.
A protector of the people; a public figure who appeals to and on behalf of the people through oratory.
The domed or vaulted apse in a cathedral housing the bishop's throne (see).
Synonym of pulpit, a platform, a place or opportunity to express one's opinion
ex: The new magazine's goal is to give a tribune to unmarried mothers.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English tributarie (“paying tribute”), from Latin tribūtārius, from tribūtum (“tribute”).

s.def: A natural water stream that flows into a larger river or other body of water.
A vein which drains into another vein.
ex: The great saphenous vein is a tributary of the femoral vein.

s.def: A nation, state, or other entity that pays tribute.
Related to the paying of tribute.
Subordinate; inferior.
ex: to grace his tributary gods

s.def: Yielding supplies of any kind; serving to form or make up, a greater object of the same kind, as a part, branch, etc.; contributing.
ex: The Ohio has many tributary streams, and is itself tributary to the Mississippi.

ety: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English tribut (14th c.), from Middle French tribut, from Latin tributum (“tribute”, literally “a thing contributed or paid”), past participle of tribuere (“to assign, allot”), usually derived from tribus (“tribe”, which see).

s.def: An acknowledgment of gratitude, respect or admiration; an accompanying gift.
ex: Please accept this as a tribute of our thanks.
the passing tribute of a sigh

s.def: A payment made by one nation to another in submission.
ex: The Ancient Romans made their conquered countries pay tribute.

s.def: Extortion; protection money.
A payment made by a feudal vassal to his lord.
A certain proportion of the mined ore, or of its value, given to the miner as payment.
Ellipsis of cum tribute.
To pay as tribute.
ex: Amorous Trifler, that spendeth[…]his Afternoones in discourse with Paint, or Lust, tributing most precious Minutes, to the Scepter of a Fanne.

ety: From Middle English trīcen, trice, trise (“to pull or push; to snatch away; to steal”), from Middle Dutch trīsen (“to hoist”) (modern Dutch trijsen) or Middle Low German trissen (“to trice the spritsail”); further etymology uncertain. The word is cognate with Danish trisse, tridse (“to haul with a pulley”), Low German trissen, tryssen, drisen, drysen (“to wind up, trice”), German trissen, triezen (“to annoy or torment”).

s.def: To pull, to pull out or away, to pull sharply.
ex: The tent is made of light, close, unbleached duck, […] A window, six inches square, is fitted at the upper end with a flap to trice up or haul down.

s.def: To drag or haul, especially with a rope; specifically (nautical) to haul or hoist and tie up by means of a rope.
ex: ... the fold of his double chin hung like a bag triced up close under the hinge of his jaw.

s.def: Now only in the phrase in a trice: a very short time; the blink of an eye, an instant, a moment.
ex: He saw a Turnkey in a trice / Unfetter a troublesome blade;
And in a trice he has clambered onto the kitchen dresser and is reaching for the top shelf.

s.def: A pulley, a windlass (“form of winch for lifting heavy weights, comprising a cable or rope wound around a cylinder”).

ety: From Latin triceps (“triple-headed”), from trēs (“three”) + caput (“head”). See there for more details.

s.def: Any muscle having three heads.
Specifically, the triceps brachii.
ex: Kickbacks work the triceps muscle at the back of your arm. Exercising these muscles helps eliminate arm jiggle.

ety: From tricho- + -iasis.

s.def: Ingrown eyelash.

ety: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek τρίχινος (tríkhinos, “of hair”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

s.def: Any of several parasitic roundworms, of the genus Trichinella, that infect the intestines and cause trichinosis

ety: tri- + chloro- + ethylene (“ethyl (“eth- + -yl”) + -ene”)

s.def: The unsaturated chlorinated hydrocarbon CCl₂=CHCl used as an industrial solvent and formerly as an anaesthetic.
ex: The nurse gave the woman in labour trichloroethylene, a chemical also used to clean metal parts.

s.def: chloroform

ety: From Ancient Greek τρῐχός (trĭkhós, “hair”).

s.def: Forming words related to hair.

ety: From French trichome, from New Latin trichoma, from Ancient Greek τρίχωμα (tríkhōma), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) or independently from tricho- + -ome. Doublet of trichoma.

s.def: A hair- or scale-like extension of the epidermis of a plant.
Hairlike structures found in some microscopic organisms and algae.
A row of cells formed by successive cell divisions.

ety: From tricho- + -osis.

s.def: Any disease or abnormality of the hair.
An overgrowth of hair; hairiness.

ety: From tricho- + Ancient Greek τίλλω (tíllō, “I pull out, pluck”) + -mania.

s.def: A medical disorder where someone compulsively pulls their own hair out.

ety: From Ancient Greek τριχοτομία (trikhotomía), from τρίχα (tríkha) + τόμος (tómos) + -ία (-ía).

s.def: Division or separation into three groups or pieces.

the property of an order relation whereby, given an ordered pair of elements (of a given algebraic structure), exactly one of these is true: the first element is 'less than' the second one, the second is 'less than' the first, or the two elements are equal.
ex: [A linear order] obeys the following trichotomy law[.]

ety: From Middle English trikke, from Old Northern French trique (related to Old French trichier (“to defraud, act dishonestly, conceal, deceive, cheat”); > modern French tricher), itself possibly from Middle High German trechen (“to launch a shot at, play a trick on”), or one of its derivatives (e.g. Middle High German ūftrechen (“to do something to someone, hurt someone”), vertrechen (“to conceal, get over on someone”), zuotrechen (“to obtain falsely or deceitfully, wangle, finagle”), etc.); yet t…

s.def: Something designed to fool, dupe, outsmart, mislead or swindle.
ex: It was just a trick to say that the house was underpriced.
He played a trick on his sister as April Fool's Day.

s.def: A single element of a magician's (or any variety entertainer's) act; a magic trick.
ex: And for my next trick, I will pull a wombat out of a duffel bag.

s.def: To fool; to cause to believe something untrue; to deceive.
ex: You tried to trick me when you said that house was underpriced.
I was once tricked into believing I had left my phone in the locker.

s.def: An entertaining difficult physical action.
ex: That's a nice skateboard, but can you do any tricks on it?
Yo-yo tricks involving sleeping the yo-yo (like "walking the dog" and "rocking the baby") cannot be performed in space.

s.def: An effective, clever or quick way of doing something.
ex: tricks of the trade; what's the trick of getting this chair to fold up?

s.def: Mischievous or annoying behavior; a prank.
ex: the tricks of boys
They played a crude trick on the teacher.

s.def: A particular habit or manner; a peculiarity; a trait.
ex: a trick of drumming with the fingers; a trick of frowning
The trick of that voice I do well remember.

s.def: A knot, braid, or plait of hair.
ex: I cannot tell , but it stirs me more than all your court curls , or your spangles , or your tricks

s.def: A sequence in which each player plays a card and a winning play is determined.
ex: I was able to take the second trick with the queen of hearts.
And now (as oft in some distemper'd state) / On one nice trick depends the gen'ral fate!

s.def: A sex act, chiefly one performed for payment; an act of prostitution.
ex: turn a trick
You lied to me, Leon. It was a rough trick.

s.def: A form of a light-hearted request by which children obtain candy on Halloween while wearing themed costumes.

A question that attempts to elicit an answer in a certain way, often a misleading or incorrect one, or a question that lacks a clear answer, conceals its true intent, or obscures an underlying difficulty.
A complex question, whose wording hinders the ability to answer it correctly.

ety: From trick + -ish.

s.def: Using tricks or trickery.

ety: From Middle English triklen, likely a rebracketing (e.g. teres strikled > teerys trikled (“tears trickled”)) of Middle English striklen (“to trickle”), equivalent to strike + -le. For other similar cases of incorrect division, see also apron, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, umpire.

s.def: A very thin river.
ex: The brook had shrunk to a mere trickle.

s.def: A very thin flow; the sound of such a flow.
ex: The tap of the washbasin in my bedroom is leaking and the trickle drives me mad at night.

s.def: to pour a liquid in a very thin stream, or so that drops fall continuously.
ex: The doctor trickled some iodine on the wound.

s.def: to flow in a very thin stream or drop continuously.
ex: Here the water just trickles along, but later it becomes a torrent.
The film was so bad that people trickled out of the cinema before its end.
Her white night-dress was smeared with blood, and a thin stream trickled down the man's bare chest which was shown by his torn-open dress.

s.def: To move or roll slowly.
ex: They gather one by one, trickling into the shady courtyard, the familiar hum of Mass. Ave. wafting in from behind brick buildings and iron gates.
Their only shot of the first period was a long-range strike from top-scorer Ebanks-Blake which trickled tamely wide.

ety: Etymology tree English trick Proto-West Germanic *-astrijā Old English -estre Middle English -estere English -ster English trickster From trick + -ster.

s.def: A fraud or cheat (person who performs a trick or hoax full of falsehoods for the purpose of unlawful gain).
ex: That shady trickster faked being a psychic advisor to spread misinformation and gain profit.
She's easy game for a trickster like him.

s.def: Any of numerous figures featuring in various mythologies and folk traditions, who use guile and secret knowledge to challenge authority and play tricks and pranks on others with their acts of trickery; any similar figure in literature.
One who plays tricks or pranks on others.
ex: A skilled trickster knows how to outsmart their enemies with ease.

s.def: One who performs tricks (parts of a magician act or entertainingly difficult physical actions).
ex: Our fellow trickster will perform some impressive magic tricks tonight.

s.def: An impish or playful person.
To engage in the antics of a trickster; to play tricks.
Alternative form of ticktack (“kind of backgammon”).

ety: Etymology tree English trick Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English tricky From trick + -y.

s.def: Adept at using deception.

s.def: Relating to or associated with a prostitution trick.
ex: I don't want any of your tricky money, thank you!

ety: Borrowed from Latin tricornis (“three-horned; three-pronged”). By surface analysis, tri- + corn(er). Compare French tricorne (“three-cornered hat”). Doublet of tricorne.

s.def: A three-cornered hat, with the brim turned up.

Having three horns or similar projections.

ety: From French tricot, from tricoter (“to knit”).

s.def: A soft knit fabric.

A molar tooth that has three cusps

ety: From French tricycle. By surface analysis, tri- + cycle.

s.def: A cycle with three wheels, powered by pedals and usually intended for young children.
ex: [S]o I rode home on my brand new tricycle to find the rest of the family parked in front of the box.

s.def: An autorickshaw; A motorized cycle rickshaw (usually a roofed motorcycle with sidecar, often available for hire in the manner of a taxi)
To ride a tricycle.
ex: The child tricycled around the driveway until dark.

ety: From tri- + Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”).

Composed of three movable parts attached to a common base.

An instrument used for sampling something.

That which tries or approves; a test.

ety: From Middle English trifle, trifel, triful, trefle, truyfle, trufful, from Old French trufle (“mockery”), a byform of trufe, truffe (“deception”), of uncertain origin.

s.def: An English dessert made from a mixture of thick custard, fruit, sponge cake, jelly and whipped cream.
ex: It is interesting to watch the surface joviality on screen while racism is layered between courses like soggy trifles.

s.def: Anything that is of little importance or worth.
ex: Trifles light as air / Are to the jealous confirmation strong / As proofs of holy writ.

s.def: A very small amount (of something).
ex: This Line leaves out […] Poplar and Black-vvall, vvhich are indeed contiguous, a Trifle of Ground excepted, and very populous.

ex: You must not trifle with her affections.
[…] Do not believe / That, from the sense of all civility, / I thus would play and trifle with your reverence:

s.def: To act, speak, or otherwise behave with jest.
ex: […] playing and trifling are completely banished out of my mind […]

s.def: To inconsequentially toy with something.
ex: Mr. Micawber, leaning back in his chair, trifled with his eye-glass and cast his eyes up at the ceiling […]

s.def: To squander or waste.
ex: As it was, he did nothing with much zeal, but sport; and his time was otherwise trifled away, without benefit from books or anything else.
You who have known neither sorrow nor pleasure; who have trifled your life away!

s.def: To make a trifle of, to make trivial.

s.def: Trivial, or of little importance.

s.def: The act of one who trifles; frivolous behaviour.

Compare Early Medieval Latin troppus. Doublet of troupe, and possibly also of thorp, dorp, and trip. Cognate with German Dorf (“village”).

s.def: A collection of people; a number; a multitude (in general).

To march on; to go forward in haste.
To move or march as if in a crowd.
ex: The children trooped into the room.

ety: From troop + -er, from French troupe. The sense of “one who endures adversity” comes from trouper (“member of an acting troupe”) but through assimilation with the sense of “soldier” has come to be usually spelled “trooper”.

ety: From Latin tropus, from Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “a manner, style, turn, way; a trope or figure of speech; a mode in music; a mode or mood in logic”), related to τροπή (tropḗ, “solstice; trope; turn”) and τρέπειν (trépein, “to turn”); compare turn of phrase. Mathematical senses.
Musical senses.
Philosophical senses.
Senses relating chiefly to art or literature.

ety: From Ancient Greek τροφικός (trophikós, “pertaining to food or nourishment”), from τροφή (trophḗ, “food”).

Of or pertaining to growth.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”).

s.def: nourish; nourishment.

ety: From Middle French trophée, from Latin trophaeum (“a sign of victory, a monument”), tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “a rout, a turning of an enemy”). Doublet of tropæum.

s.def: Any emblem of success; a status symbol.

s.def: An object, usually in the form of a statuette, cup, or shield, awarded for success in a competition or to mark a special achievement.
ex: He won the trophy in a running competition.

s.def: An object taken as a prize by a hunter, or a conqueror or belligerent, especially one that is displayed.
ex: The set of antlers which hung on the wall was his prized trophy.

ex: A trophy from this murder would have been of great importance.

An animal killed by a trophy hunter that usually has its parts sold on the black market.
To adorn (someone) with trophies.
To win a trophy in a competition.

ety: From Late Latin tropicus (“of or pertaining to the solstice, as a noun, one of the tropics”), from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”).
