s.def: A change from one thing to its opposite, or from a situation to the reverse.
A reversal of a decision or opinion etc; a change of mind or flip-flop.
A three-point turn or any similar act of turning around, with the same outcome, regardless of how many repeated forward-reverse maneuvers it takes.
A merry-go-round.

ety: Deverbal from turn around.

s.def: Translations
The act of turning to face in the other direction.
ex: The basketball player made a turnaround jump shot.

s.def: A reversal of policy.
The carrying out of a task; the time required to carry it out.
ex: They tried to reduce their turnaround on incoming paperwork.
They tried to reduce their turnaround time on incoming paperwork. [noun adjunct form]

s.def: A turnabout; a reversal of circumstances.
A series of sketches of a character as seen from different angles.
A cadence linking the end of a verse to the beginning of the next.
The notation for the addition of a grace note above then below a given note.
Synonym of goback.
The scheduled shutdown of an industrial plant, such as an oil rig, for maintenance and testing.

ety: From turn + buckle.

s.def: A coupling device consisting of two eyelets or other connection points connected in screw threads.
A link threaded on both ends of a short bar which is used to pull objects together.
The area at either end of a bench where the edge of the glass is padded and meets the boards at a right angle.
ex: A player who is checked into the turnbuckles may be injured.

ety: A compound of turn + coat, reportedly derived from the sometime military practice of wearing uniform coats that were lined in material of a contrasting color, and which could be worn inside out to present a different appearance.

s.def: A traitor; one who turns against a previous affiliation or allegiance.
ex: But some will cry Turncoat, and rip up old stories, / How I always pretended to be for the tories: […]

s.def: To act as a turncoat; to betray

ety: From turn + cock.

s.def: A tap or faucet that regulates the flow of a fluid.
A person employed to turn on the water for the mains, to regulate the fireplugs, etc. for a water company.
ex: 1,000 crossing-sweepers; another thousand chimney-sweeps, and the same number of turncocks and lamp-lighters;

ety: Deverbal from turn down.

s.def: A downturn.
ex: In past recessions, drugstores were virtually immune from a turndown.

s.def: A rejection.
The service of turning down the bedcovers and often leaving chocolates, etc., on the pillow.
A downward pointing extension to a vehicle muffler.
The operational range of a device.
Capable of being turned down, or decreased in intensity.
ex: a turndown lamp

s.def: Made to wear with the upper part turned down.
ex: a turndown collar

ety: From Middle English turner, torner, tornere, turnere, turnare, equivalent to turn + -er. Also from Middle English turnour, tornour, tournour, turnoure, from Old French tornour, tourneour, tourneur, tornëor (“one who fashions something by turning”).

s.def: A person who turns and shapes wood etc. on a lathe.
One who or that which turns.
A kitchen utensil used for turning food.
A variety of pigeon; a tumbler.
A very dry pitch on which the ball will turn with ease.
An acrobat or gymnast, especially (historical) a member of the German Turnvereine, German-American gymnastic clubs that also served as nationalist political groups.
An old Scottish copper coin worth two pence, issued by King James VI.

ety: Named after Henry Turner who first described the condition in 1938.

s.def: A particular genetic condition, caused by partially or completely missing an X chromosome (monosomy), that leads to sterility and other issues.

ety: From turn + -ery.

s.def: The art of fashioning solid bodies into cylindrical or other forms by means of a lathe.
Things or forms made by a turner, or in the lathe.
ex: August 20, 1761, Horace Walpole, letter to George Montagu, Esq. Chairs of wood, the seats triangular, the backs, arms, and legs loaded with turnery.

s.def: A place where lathework is carried out.
Alternative form of turnhalle.

ety: From Middle English turnyng, turnynge, from Old English tyrning, turnung, equivalent to turn + -ing.

s.def: A turn or deviation from a straight course.
ex: Take the second turning on the left.
Except for turnings with a deflated rear tire as an outerside tire, difference in the performance is small between fixed control and manual control.

s.def: At hockey, a foul committed by a player attempting to hit the ball who interposes their body between the ball and an opposing player trying to do the same.
The cutting of wood or metal on a lathe to shape it as needed.
The act of one who turns (rotates or twists).
One of the four eras, each lasting for about 21 years, that make up a saeculum according to the Strauss-Howe generational theory.
ex: Howe and Strauss predicted that in the Fourth Turning, Millennials would unite behind their president.

s.def: Shavings produced by turning something on a lathe.
ex: The turnings get into your trouser turnups!

s.def: present participle and gerund of turn
ex: The Earth is turning about its axis as we speak.
He made wooden soldiers by turning them on a hand lathe.

der: it's a long road that has no turning

s.def: A decisive point at which a significant change or historical event occurs, or at which a decision must be made.
ex: Another turning point, a fork stuck in the road / Time grabs you by the wrist, directs you where to go

s.def: A maximum or minimum on a graph.
A crossroads.
A T-junction.
A place at which one changes their direction of travel.
ex: Chicago was the turning point of my journey and I left there at midnight abroad ^([sic]) the "Chicagoan," an express of the New York Central System.

ety: From Middle English turnepe, probably from turn + Middle English nepe, from Old English nǣp, from Latin nāpus. The component turn may be due to the round shape of the plant as though turned on a lathe, or because it must be turned and twisted to be harvested. Cognate to neep. See also parsnip.

s.def: white root of Brassica rapa
The white root of a yellow-flowered plant, Brassica rapa, grown as a vegetable and as fodder for cattle.
ex: In general, beets, carrots, and turnips are all of aphrodisiac value in erotic dietary.
The turnip is one of the lordliest vegetables in the world; its broth is practically a soup in itself.

s.def: The yellow root of a related plant, the swede or Brassica napus.
The white root of Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus, also known as a daikon.
The root of the yam bean, Pachyrhizus erosus; jicama.
Clipping of turnip watch
A fool or simpleton.
To plant with turnips.
ex: This identical field has been turniped before, and to good account, in a favourable winter.

s.def: To feed or graze (livestock) on turnips.
ex: This system of turniping is found to encourage the growth and muscular development of young stock.

der: get blood out of a turnip

ety: From turn + key. (jailer): Compare typologically Russian вертуха́й (vertuxáj) (akin to верте́ть (vertétʹ)).

s.def: Ready to use without further assembly or test; supplied in a state that is ready to turn on and operate (typically refers to an assembly that is outsourced for manufacture).
ex: They wanted a turnkey solution for the entire system, but we could only provide the enclosure.
Third World countries no longer want to purchase nuclear projects on a turn-key basis; they want to receive advanced technical training as well.

s.def: A warder or jailer; a keeper of the keys in a prison.
ex: He saw the same Turnkey unfetter a man / With but little expedition, / Which put him in mind of the long debate / On the Slave-trade abolition.
'Certainly not,' said the turnkey; and the first corroborated his statement.

s.def: A system that is supplied ready to switch on and operate.
To supply a turnkey product; to supply something fully assembled and ready to use.
ex: We can sell you all the parts, or we can turnkey the entire unit.

ety: Deverbal from turn out.

s.def: The act of coming forth.
The number or proportion of people who attend or participate in an event (especially an election) or are present at a venue.
ex: Depending on the location of a restaurant, weekdays may equally experience low turnout.

s.def: A place to pull off a road.
ex: When towing a trailer, use the turnouts to let faster traffic pass.

s.def: A place where moveable rails allow a train to switch tracks; a set of points.
ex: [...] the Welwyn bottleneck will be relaid with high-speed turnouts and resignalled for reversible working.

s.def: A quitting of employment for the purpose of forcing increase of wages; a strike.
A striker.
That which is prominently brought forward or exhibited; hence, an equipage.
ex: A man with a showy carriage and horses is said to have a fine turnout.
Occasionally turnouts would be seen driven randem in circus parades.

s.def: Net quantity of produce yielded.
The act of putting out to pasture.
ex: Duties include feeding and turnout of horses.

s.def: Rotation of the leg at the hips which causes the feet and knees to turn outward, away from the front of the body.

ety: Deverbal from turn over.

s.def: The amount of money taken as sales transacted in a given period.
ex: The company had an annual turnover of $500,000.

s.def: The frequency with which stock is replaced after being used or sold, workers leave and are replaced, a property changes hands, etc.
ex: High staff-turnover can lead to low morale amongst employees.
Job dissatisfaction results in high turnover.
Those apartments have a high turnover because they are too close to the railroad tracks.

s.def: A semicircular pastry made by turning one half of a circular crust over the other, enclosing the filling (such as fruit).
ex: They only served me one apple turnover for breakfast.

s.def: A loss of possession of the ball without scoring.
ex: The Nimrods committed another dismaying turnover en route to another humiliating loss.

s.def: A measure of leg speed: the frequency with which one takes strides when running, typically given in strides per minute.
The act or result of overturning something; an upset.
ex: a bad turnover in a carriage

s.def: An act or process of turning something over.
ex: a turnover in leadership

s.def: Synonym of runover.
An apprentice, in any trade, who is handed over from one master to another to complete his time.
Capable of being turned over; designed to be turned over.
ex: a turnover collar

ety: From Middle English turnpyke (“spiked barrier across a road”), originally used to block access to such a road until a toll was paid. Equivalent to modern turn + pike (“shaft”).

s.def: A frame consisting of two bars crossing each other at right angles and turning on a post or pin, to hinder the passage of animals, but admitting a person to pass between the arms.
A gate or bar set across a road to stop carriages, animals, and sometimes people, until a toll is paid.
A winding stairway.
A beam filled with spikes to obstruct passage; a cheval de frise.
A toll road, especially a toll expressway. In some places the clipped version, pike, is used for roads without tolls.
ex: [T]here is a bundle of pawnbrokers' duplicates, those turnpike tickets on the road of poverty ...

s.def: A trajectory on a finite time interval that satisfies an optimality criterion which is associated with a cost function.
To form (a road, etc.) in the manner of a turnpike road, or into a rounded form, as the path of a road.

ety: From turn + spit.

s.def: A person employed in turning a spit for the purpose of roasting meat.
Synonym of roasting jack.
A person engaged in some menial occupation.
Ellipsis of turnspit dog.

s.def: A rotating mechanical device that controls and counts passage between public areas, especially one that only allows passage after a charge has been paid.
ex: an efficient system for funneling crowds through turnstiles
The fare was fixed at 2d., irrespective of distance, and was paid by passengers on passing through turnstiles at each station.

s.def: A similar device in a footpath to allow people through one at a time while preventing the passage of cattle.
The ⊢ symbol used to represent logical entailment (deducibility relation), especially of the syntactic type; i.e., syntactic consequence. (Such symbol can be read as "prove(s)" or "give(s)". )

ety: From turn + table.

s.def: A circular rotating platform.
To play (a record) using a turntable.
ex: Rik Shaw of Deadly Dragon Soundsystem continues his weekly residency by turntabling the rudest Jamaican dance records ever pressed.

s.def: To rotate or turn around using, or as if using, a turntable.
To manipulate sound using turntables; to perform turntablism; to scratch
ex: We particularly like hovering next to DJ Sid Wilson and seeing how he spends the large chunks of time where he's not turntabling.

ety: Deverbal from turn up.

s.def: Alternative form of turn-up.

ety: From German turnen (“to exercise”) + Verein (“a union”).

s.def: A gymnastic or athletic club, originally those promoting German culture. They originated in the 19th century and spread from Germany to the USA, where a small number still exist, at least in name.

ety: Borrowed from Uyghur تۇرپان (turpan).

s.def: A prefecture-level city of the Xinjiang autonomous region, China.

ety: From Middle English terebentyne, terbentyne, turbentine, from Old French terbentine, turbentine, Latin terebinthina, from Ancient Greek τερεβινθίνη (terebinthínē), the feminine form of τερεβινθινος (terebinthinos, “terebinthine”, adjective), from τερέβινθος (terébinthos, “terebinth tree”, noun). Related to terpene and terpin; etymologically equivalent to terebinth + -ine.

s.def: A volatile essential oil now obtained from such oleoresin of from the wood of pine trees by steam distillation; a complex mixture of monoterpenes; now used as a solvent and paint thinner.
Any oleoresin secreted by the wood or bark of certain trees.
A turpentine tree (genus Syncarpia).
ex: Turpentine timber was obtained from the forests outside Maryborough and Townsville, and shipped by rail and landing craft to Hayman Island.

s.def: To drain resin from (a tree) for use in making turpentine.

ety: From Medieval Latin turpethum, from Arabic تُرْبِد (turbid), from Persian تربد (torbed), from Sanskrit त्रिपुटा (tripuṭā), त्रिपुट (tripuṭa), literally “triplicated”, names of several plants.

s.def: Operculina turpethum (obs. syn. Convolvulus turpethum, Ipomea turpethum, Merremia turpethum), a plant in the morning glory family.
A heavy yellow powder with chemical formula Hg₃O₂SO₄.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French turpitude, from Latin turpitūdō (“baseness, infamy”), from turpis (“foul, base”).

s.def: Inherent baseness, depravity or wickedness; corruptness and evilness.
ex: As for the moral turpitude that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror.

s.def: An act evident of such depravity.

ety: From Middle French turquoise, from Old French (pierre) turquoise (“Turkish (stone)”), from turc + -ois. The stone, mined near Nishapur in the Khorasan region of Persia, was originally brought to Europe through Turkey. Doublet of Turkish. Compare typologically copper (<< Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros, “Cyprus”)).

s.def: A pale greenish-blue colour, like that of the gemstone.
gemstone
A sky-blue, greenish-blue, or greenish-gray semi-precious gemstone.
Having a pale greenish-blue colour.
Made of turquoise (the gemstone).

ety: From Middle English touret, from Old French torete (French tourette), diminutive of tour (“tower”), from Latin turris. Doublet of tor, tourelle, and tower. See tower.

s.def: A little tower, frequently a merely ornamental structure at one of the corners of a building or castle.
ex: Their Victorian house had three turrets and a large amount of gingerbread trim.

s.def: A siege tower; a movable building, of a square form, consisting of ten or even twenty stories and sometimes one hundred and twenty cubits high, usually moved on wheels, and employed in approaching a fortified place, for carrying soldiers, engines, ladders, casting bridges, and other necessaries.
A tower-like solder post on a turret board (a circuit board with posts instead of holes).
An armoured, rotating gun installation on a fort, ship, aircraft, or armoured fighting vehicle.
The elevated central portion of the roof of a passenger car, with sides that are pierced for light and ventilation.
A turret head.
The central conical ornament atop a spinning roulette wheel.

ety: Latin turricula (“small tower, turret”).

s.def: Furnished with, or formed like, a small turret or turrets; somewhat turreted.
ex: turriculate shell
turriculate species
turriculate shell

ety: Modification of Middle English tortou, tortu, from Old French tortüe (under the influence of Middle English turtel, turtur (“turtledove”), see Etymology 2 below), from Old Occitan tortuga (compare Spanish tortuga), the same source of tortoise (see there for more). Displaced native Old English byrdling (See birdling).

s.def: land or marine reptile with a shell
Any land, aquatic, or semi-aquatic reptile of the order Testudines, characterised by a protective shell enclosing its body. See also tortoise.
ex: A unique anti-aphrodisiac was the heart of a turtle carried in a wolf's skin. It prevented a person from ever being tempted amorously.

s.def: Senses resembling a turtle in protection
Senses resembling a turtle in shape or movement
Senses resembling a turtle in slowness
To flip over onto the back or top; to turn upside down.
ex: Were speeding when car turtled […] Auto crashed into curb and turtled.

s.def: To move along slowly.
ex: We turtled along in Manitoba, back into the heart of the prairies.

s.def: To hunt turtles, especially in the water.
ex: Of these, 80 turtled (65%), 26 hunted and turtled (20%), and 18 hunted (15%).

s.def: Ellipsis of turtle head (“to struggle to hold back an imminent bowel movement”).
To build up a large defense force and strike only occasionally, rather than going for an offensive strategy.

ety: From Middle English turtildove, turteldoufe (cognate with Old High German turtultūba, turtulatūba, turtiltūba, Middle High German turteltūbe, türteltūbe, German Turteltaube; German Low German Turtelduuv, Dutch tortelduif, Faroese turtildúgva, Icelandic turtildúfa), Danish turteldue, Norwegian Bokmål turteldue, Norwegian Nynorsk turteldue, Swedish turturduva. The first element is from Latin turtur (“turtledove”) (compare the archaic synonym turtle (“turtle dove (bird)”); the word is not related…

s.def: Any of several (species of) birds, called by this traditional name, mainly in the genus Streptopelia, of the family Columbidae (doves and pigeons, which also included the extinct passenger pigeon, dodo, and solitaire).
A lover, one half of a couple.
ex: Out for their evening constitutional. A lovely pair of turtledoves. Around the jolly corner, and off to the park.

ety: From turtle + back.

s.def: Anything having the shape of a turtle's back (that is, its shell).
ex: Up he went on concrete stairs that were eroded to turtlebacks and slippery with evening's frost […]

s.def: A convex deck at the bow or stern of a vessel, designed to shed seawater quickly.

An armor layout with an armored deck which slopes downwards towards the sides of the ship and connects to the lower edge of the main belt armor, designed to deflect shells striking the ship on trajectories close to horizontal.
A primitive stone celt of a form suggesting the back of a turtle.
A library binding of a mass market paperback with a generic hardcover.
ex: When you order Turtleback Books from Baker & Taylor, you can be assured you get Turtlebacks!

s.def: Any plant of the genus Psathyrotes of annual and perennial forbs and low subshrubs native to dry areas of southwestern North America.
Alternative spelling of turtle dove.
A mythological bird of prey, mostly depicted as a falcon, in Hungarian and Turkic tradition.

ety: From Middle English Tuscan, from Late Latin Tuscānus (“belonging to the Tusci”), a people of ancient Italy, from Tuscus, earlier *Truscus, shortened form of Etruscus (“Etruscan”).

s.def: A native or inhabitant of Tuscany, Italy.
A local variety of Italian spoken in Tuscany, on which Standard Italian is largely based.

ety: Late 14c., from Middle English Tuscan, Tuscane, from Old French Toscane or Italian Toscana, from Late Latin Tuscānus (“belonging to the Tusci”), a people of ancient Italy, from Tuscus, earlier *Truscus, shortened form of Etruscus (“Etruscan”).

s.def: An administrative region of Italy, located north of Lazio and south of Emilia-Romagna.

ety: From Middle English tusshe, tusche, tussch, tossche, tosch, from Old English tūsc, from Proto-Germanic *tunþskaz. Doublet of tusk.

s.def: A tusk.
ex: […] he was still a majestic-looking pig, with a wise and benevolent appearance in spite of the fact that his tushes had never been cut.

s.def: A small tusk sometimes found on the female Indian elephant.
The buttocks.
ex: Are you gonna tell Glenn?...About you and that kid, and him squeezing your tush.

s.def: An exclamation of rebuke or scorn.
ex: "Tush, Sir Minstrel," replied the archer, displeased at Bertram's interference, […]

s.def: Nonsense; tosh.
To express contempt; rebuke.
To pull or drag a heavy object such as a tree or log.
Clipping of tusheroon, itself an alternative form of tosheroon.

ex: The massive tusker leading the herd stopped in his tracks. His ears went out, his long sinuous trunk up.

s.def: A tool used in peat cutting, a type of turf spade similar to a cascrom.

ety: From Latin tussis (“cough”).

s.def: A cough.
ex: Except of my coffin, / For what can I else with this horrible tussis?
As George whittled the lengthy wood, his tussis nearly cured, he found himself surrounded by curious lads and lasses.

ety: From Latin tussis + -ive.

s.def: Related to, caused by, or accompanied by a cough

ety: Related to tousle.

s.def: A physical fight or struggle.
ex: ..., two young men—field hands—got into a tussle with a white man.

s.def: A conflict, an argument, a disagreement.
To have a tussle.
ex: The two sets of fans were tussling before the game.

ety: Uncertain. Likely from or related to tusk + -ock (diminutive suffix). Compare Middle High German zūsach (“thicket”), a derivative of Middle High German zūse (“lock of hair”). Compare also Scottish Gaelic dosag (“little tuft”).

s.def: A tuft or clump of green grass or similar verdure, forming a small hillock.
ex: An Indian grazing ground is all rocks and scrub and tussocks and little ravines, among which the herds scatter and disappear.

s.def: Tussock grass.
ex: I yearned, painfully, for […] a sight and touch of a hillside covered with golden tussock.

ety: Imitative.

s.def: Tut tut; an expression of disapproval.
Hush; be silent.
To make a tut tut sound of disapproval.
A tutorial.
A hassock.
A piece of work.
Rubbish.
ex: Such stupidness is mad 'cause nothing underfoot comes to nothing less to add to a load of old tut.
Cracking excuse: credible, watertight and yet patently a load of old tut.
“Well there's a load of old tut in the cupboard next to Felicia's room,” she said grudgingly.

s.def: To work by the piece; to carry out tut-work.
To dance in the style known as tutting.
Used to indicate disapproval, disappointment, or discontent.
An expression of annoyance or impatience.

ety: Borrowed from Egyptian i-mn:n-t-w&t-anx (twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn, literally “Living Image of Amun”). The variant spellings of the final vowel are taken from variant forms of the name of the god Amun as found in various different sources: u from Coptic ⲁⲙⲟⲩⲛ (amoun), o from Ancient Greek Ἄμμων (Ámmōn), and e from the purely conventional system of Egyptological pronunciation.

s.def: Ancient Egyptian pharaoh known for his young age and his tomb, which was preserved intact to the modern age.

ety: From Latin tūtēla (“a watching, guardianship, protection”) + -age, from tuērī (“to watch, guard”). See tuition.

s.def: The act of guarding, protecting, or guiding.
ex: the king's right of seigniory and tutelage
The childhood of the European nations was passed under the tutelage of the clergy.

s.def: The state of being under a guardian or a tutor; the care or protection enjoyed; being a ward or a tutee.
Instruction; teaching; guidance; being a tutor.

ety: From Latin tūtēlārius (“guardian”), from tūtēla (“tutelage, guardianship; dependent, client”) + -ārius (suffix denoting an agent of use); analysable as tutelar + -ary.

s.def: Relating to guardianship or protection.
ex: When a minor is involved, tutelary powers frequently accompany powers of attorney.
In Antwerp, for instance, as late as the sixteenth century Priapus was the tutelary god of the city.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a guardian.
ex: My uncle is always happy to discharge his tutelary responsibilities towards me.

s.def: Having the qualities of a tutor.
A deity or spirit serving as a guardian or protector of a place, person, culture, etc.; a tutelar, a tutelary deity.

ety: From Middle English tutour, from Old French tuteur (French tuteur), from Latin tūtor (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from tueor (“protect”); see tuition.

s.def: One who teaches another (usually called a student, learner, or tutee) in a one-on-one or small-group interaction.
ex: He passed the difficult class with help from his tutor.

s.def: A university officer responsible for students in a particular hall.
A homeroom.
One who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate; a guardian.
To instruct or teach, especially an individual or small group.
ex: To help pay her tuition, the college student began to tutor high school students in calculus and physics.

s.def: To treat with authority or sternness.
A card that allows one to search one's deck for one or more other cards.
ex: here are some tutor cards i thought would be interesting.

s.def: To fetch a card from one's deck.
ex: Any instant that you move to the board can *only* be tutored for with Cunning Wish.

ety: From Old French toutesaine.

s.def: Hypericum androsaemum, a Eurasian perennial shrub.
ex: The healing Tutsan

ety: From Italian tutti, from Latin totus (“all”).

s.def: All together. Indicates that the remainder of a group should join in playing after a solo or other passage with a reduced number of voices.
All together; with all playing at once.
ex: a tutti passage

s.def: A passage in which all members of an orchestra are playing
ex: Even so, the orchestra endowed tuttis with a positively radiant glow.

ety: From Sicilian tutti frutti (“all fruits”), so attested in 1838 for a kind of sorbet.

s.def: A variety of ice cream (or, formerly, other confection) that contains chopped candied fruit.
Candied raw papaya (unripened papaya).
A male homosexual.
ex: Yeah, hell, yeah. And the men, they're mostly tutti-fruttis.

s.def: A type of flavored cocaine.
A type of inhalable, powdered drug.

ety: From French tutie; compare Spanish tutía, atutía, from Latin tutia, from Arabic تُوتِيَاء (tūtiyāʔ), from Classical Persian توتیا (tūtyā), from Sanskrit तुत्था (tutthā).

s.def: A powdered form of impure zinc oxide used for polishing.

ety: Borrowed from French tutu, from cucu (“bum, bottom”), playful reduplication of cul (“arse”).

s.def: A ballet skirt made of layered stiff but light netting.
ex: The ballet dancer representing the swan wore a white tutu.

s.def: Any of certain members of genus Coriaria of shrubs and trees found in New Zealand, including Coriaria arborea and Coriaria pottsiana, used by the Maori to make a sweetener, but toxic when not properly prepared.

Sometimes even Greek shipping tycoons run out of money.

s.def: A business simulator game, typically involving building and managing some form of infrastructure.

A game involving the use of a base to generate bricks and cash (similar to an idle game or clicker game), which can then be used to purchase upgrades and expand. Common within the massively multiplayer online game platform Roblox.
ex: Tycoons / A game in which users build up some sort of business by earning money over time and then using that money on upgrades.
In most tycoons, you will find an automatic machine called a dropper, which is used for producing bricks.
“What should we play? Adopt Me, a tycoon, SCP, an obby?”

s.def: The first placer of Tycoon.

ety: From Middle English tike, tyke, from Old Norse tík (“female dog”), from Proto-Germanic *tīkō. Compare Icelandic tík, Faroese tík, and Swedish tik, all meaning “bitch, female dog”.

s.def: small child
A mongrel dog.
A small child, especially a cheeky or mischievous one.
ex: Manipulative little tyke I was.

s.def: An uncultured, crude and unrefined or uncouth ill-bred person.
A person from Yorkshire; a Yorkshireman or Yorkshirewoman.

ety: From Medieval Latin tympanum.

s.def: A piece of cloth padding placed under the platen of a letterpress to distribute the pressure on the sheet being printed.
ex: As the pressman returns the inkballs to the inkstone, the journeyman closes the frisket and tympan.

s.def: The stretched membrane of a drum.
A percussion instrument consisting of a hollow cylinder with such a membrane at each end.
A tympanum.
The tympanum of the ear.
ex: But soon I grew used to these sounds, and then I understood as well as ever, that is to say fully one half of what won its way past my tympan.

ety: Etymology tree English tympanum Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English tympanic From tympanum + -ic.

s.def: Of, relating to, or resembling a drum.
Relating to the tympanum, eardrum or middle ear.
Resonant.

ety: Coined based on Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon).

s.def: A distended abdomen as a result of an accumulation of gas.

ety: From tympan- + -itis.

s.def: Synonym of myringitis.

ety: Borrowed from Latin tympanum (“a drum, timbrel, tambourine; the eardrum”). Doublet of timbre, timpani, timbal, and tymbal.

s.def: A vertical recessed triangular space between the sides of a pediment, typically decorated.
ex: It was a black-and-white picture of a Romanesque doorway, with flanking saints and a lively Last Judgement in the tympanum […].

s.def: A drum.
Any of various anatomic structures in various animals with analogy to a drum head:
ex: When he came around, the star sound was gone. The ringing it left in his tympana was a great confusion.

s.def: A drum-shaped wheel with spirally curved partitions by which water is raised to the axis when the wheel revolves with the lower part of the circumference submerged; used for raising water, as for irrigation.

ety: Coined based on Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon).

s.def: The sound made by beating a drum.
Tympanites (distention of the abdomen).
Inflation; conceit; bombast; turgidness.
ex: Dr. Johnson, for his triads and his antithetic balances, he taxes more than once with a plethoric and tautologic tympany of sentence

ety: From Middle English type (“symbol, figure, emblem”), from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).

s.def: A grouping based on shared characteristics; a class.
ex: This type of plane can handle rough weather more easily than that type of plane.

s.def: To enter text or commands into a computer using a keyboard.
An individual considered typical of its class, one regarded as typifying a certain profession, environment, etc.
ex: "I just peeked out toward the restaurant and there are a lot of Navy types in there. I'd hate for you to get in trouble on your last night in Europe."

s.def: An individual that represents the ideal for its class; an embodiment.
ex: Altogether he was the type of low ruffianism — as ill-conditioned a looking brute as ever ginned a hare.

s.def: A letter or character used for printing, historically a cast or engraved block.
ex: The headline was set in bold type.

s.def: Something, often a specimen, selected as an objective anchor to connect a scientific name to a taxon; this need not be representative or typical.
ex: ...thus Stearn has designated Linnaeus as the type specimen of Homo sapiens

s.def: Preferred sort of person; sort of person that one is attracted to.
ex: We can't get along: he's just not my type.
He was exactly her type.

s.def: A blood group.
A word that occurs in a text or corpus irrespective of how many times it occurs, as opposed to a token.
An event or person that prefigures or foreshadows a later event - commonly an Old Testament event linked to Christian times.

ety: From type + face.

s.def: The particular design of some type, font, or a font family.
The surface of type which inked, or the impression it makes.

ety: From type + script.

s.def: typewritten material, especially such a copy of a manuscript
A file containing a replay of commands typed into a terminal, which can then be automatically typed by a program later on.
To transcribe into typewritten form.

ety: Blend of type (“value constraint”) + JavaScript.

s.def: A scripting programming language that is a strongly-typed superset of JavaScript.

ety: From type + setter.

s.def: A person who sets type; an employee in a printshop who manually selected pieces of movable type and assembled them for printing.
A machine that combines type in the correct order for printing.
The setting of written material into type.

ety: Back-formation from typewriter.

s.def: To type using a typewriter.

ety: From type + writer.

s.def: A device, at least partially mechanical, used to print text by pressing keys that cause type to be impressed through an inked ribbon onto paper.
One who uses a typewriter; a typist.
ex: The typewriter got up and disappeared out a back door, and soon she come back with a man, and he said, "Can I be of some help, Mr. Higgens?"

s.def: A machine gun or submachine gun (from the noise it makes when firing).
ex: The battle had opened in earnest. From the wooded ridge came in reply the clacking of "typewriters,” and bullets whined over our heads.
Fortunately we were on the edge of a shallow shell hole when the sentry caught our movements and Fritz cut loose with the "typewriters."

s.def: A prank in which fingers are jabbed roughly onto someone's chest followed by striking them over the ear in imitation of using an old-fashioned typewriter.

ety: From type + writing.

s.def: The act, or the skill, of using a typewriter.
The material produced by a typewriter; typescript.
ex: Older typewriters produced typewritings in which the horizontal space allocated for each character was precisely the same.

s.def: present participle and gerund of typewrite
Alternative form of typhl-.

ety: From typhus + -oid.

s.def: Characterised by or relating to typhus.
Ellipsis of typhoid fever.
ex: Typhoid may not worry people as it once did, but it still affects more than 20 million people a year around the world.

s.def: An illness caused by the bacterium serovar Salmonella Typhi. Not to be confused with typhus.
ex: The great French microbiologist Louis Pasteur [...] lost three of his five children to typhoid fever.

ety: English texts mention typhon, tiphon as a Greek word for "whirlwind" since at least the 1550s, referring to Ancient Greek τυφῶν (tuphôn), τυφώς (tuphṓs, “whirlwind”) (the latter attested since Aeschylus), Τυφῶν (Tuphôn, “Typhon, father of the winds”). (French typhon (“whirlwind”) is said to be attested since 1504.) However, the first use of it as an English word for a whirlwind or storm dates to 1588, in the spelling Touffon, in the specific sense "giant storm in the Pacific"; this sense first…

s.def: A weather phenomenon in the northwestern Pacific that is precisely equivalent to a hurricane except for its geographical region, typically resulting in wind speeds of 64 knots (119 km/h) or above. Equivalent to a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and Indonesia and Australia.
ex: Near-synonyms: cyclone (narrow sense), hurricane

s.def: A severe tropical cyclone; an intense, rotating storm.
To swirl like a hurricane.

ety: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-, extended form of *dʰew- (“scatter like dust”).

s.def: Any of several similar diseases, characterised by high recurrent fever, caused by Rickettsia bacteria. Not to be confused with typhoid fever.
ex: Typhoid and typhus have similar names and symptoms, but are different diseases.

ety: From Late Latin typicalis, from Latin typicus (“typical”), from Ancient Greek τυπικός (tupikós, “of or pertaining to a type, conformable, typical”), from τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), equivalent to typic + -al and type + -ical.

s.def: Capturing the overall sense of a thing.
Characteristically representing something by form, group, idea or type.
Normal, average; to be expected.
Of a lower taxon, containing the type of the higher taxon.
ex: Celticecis species are definitely known only from the typical subgenus of Celtis, distributed through much of the Holarctic Region.

s.def: Anything that is typical, normal, or standard.
ex: Antipsychotic drugs can be divided into typicals and atypicals.
Among the moths, typicals were more common than melanics.

s.def: To embody, exemplify; to represent by a form, image, model, or resemblance.
ex: His attitude typifies the attitude of young people today.

s.def: To portray stereotypically.
ex: The angry captain typified all new sailors as incompetent.

s.def: To serve as a typical or reference specimen of.
ex: The chosen specimen typifies plants belonging to that species.

ety: By surface analysis, type + -ing.

s.def: The act of one who types on a keyboard.
Assignment or classification by type.
ex: Near-synonyms: classifying, categorizing; classification, categorization; sorting

ety: Etymology tree English type Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English typist From type + -ist.

s.def: A person who types, a clerical worker who writes letters, etc., using a typewriter.

ety: Clipping of typographical error.

s.def: A typographical error.
ex: Near-synonyms: misprint; slip of the pen, lapsus calami, lapsus plumæ
Sorry, I meant to say “buy a SODA”—“sofa” was a typo.

s.def: To make a typographical error.
A compositor; a typographer.
Alternative form of taipo.

ety: From New Latin typographicus + -al.

s.def: Pertaining to typography or printing.
Produced by typography; printed.

ety: Etymology tree English typographical Middle English -ly English -ly English typographically From typographical + -ly.

s.def: In a typographical manner.
ex: Typographically the tables are pleasing and easy to read.

ety: From French typographie from Medieval Latin typographia from Ancient Greek τυπογράφος (tupográphos, “certified copy”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). By surface analysis, type + -o- + -graphy.

s.def: The art or practice of setting and arranging type; typesetting.
The practice or process of printing with type.
The appearance and style of typeset matter.

ety: From Old Norse Týr, from Proto-Germanic *Tīwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dyew- (“god”). Doublet of Tiw.

s.def: The Norse god of war, identifiable with Tiu or Tiw.

ety: From French tyrannicide, from Middle French tyrannicide, from Latin tyrannicīda. Equivalent to tyrant + -cide.

s.def: The killing of a tyrant.
Someone who kills a tyrant.

ety: From Middle French tyranniser, equivalent to tyranny + -ize.

s.def: To oppress (someone).
To rule as a tyrant.
ex: The prince tyrannized over his subjects.
What? will they tyrannize vpon the Church?
General Secretary Xi is not destined to tyrannize inside and outside of China forever, unless we allow it.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos) Pre-Greekbor. Ancient Greek σαύρα (saúra) Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros)bor. Translingual -saurus Translingual Tyrannosaurusbor. English tyrannosaur Borrowed from translingual Tyrannosaurus. Doublet of tyrannosaurus

s.def: Any large bipedal carnivorous dinosaur, of the family Tyrannosauridae, that lived in North America during the Cretaceous period.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos)bor. Latin tyrannus Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English tyrannous From Latin tyrannus (“tyrant”) + English -ous.

s.def: Tyrannical, despotic or oppressive.
ex: […] that Elfe, That man and beast with powre imperious Subdeweth to his kingdome tyrannous:
As life wears on and finds no rest, The individual in each breast Is tyrannous to sunder them.

ety: Inherited from Middle English tirannye, from Old French tyrannie, from Medieval Latin tyrannia, tyrania, from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía, “tyranny”), from τύραννος (túrannos, “lord, master, sovereign, tyrant”).

s.def: A government in which a single ruler (a tyrant) has absolute power, or this system of government; especially, one that acts cruelly and unjustly.
The office or jurisdiction of an absolute ruler.
Absolute power, or its use.
A system of government in which power is exercised on behalf of the ruler or ruling class, without regard to the wishes of the governed.
ex: Control, dispossession, violence, and tyranny are not “defensive”: they are part of an organized, ongoing aggression.

s.def: Extreme severity or rigour.

ety: From Middle English tyraunt, tiraunt, tyrant, tyrante, from Old French tyrant, from the addition of a terminal -t to tiran (cp. French tyran) via a back-formation related to the development of French present participles out of the Latin -ans form, from Latin tyrannus (“despot”), from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “usurper, monarch, despot”), of uncertain origin.

s.def: A despot; a ruler who governs unjustly, cruelly, or harshly.
ex: I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe. A Foe to Tyrants, and my Countries Friend.

s.def: A usurper; one who gains power and rules extralegally, distinguished from kings elevated by election or succession.
ex: To proue him Tyrant, this reason may suffice, That Henry liueth still.

s.def: Any monarch or governor.
ex: Cassius... set tyrants over all Syria.

s.def: Any person who abuses the power of position or office to treat others unjustly, cruelly, or harshly.
ex: A plague vpon the Tyrant that I serue
[…] a sad tyrant, as my friends the Democrats sometimes are.

s.def: A villain; a person or thing who uses strength or violence to treat others unjustly, cruelly, or harshly.
ex: I was a blasphemar, and a persecuter, and a tyraunt.
A pike (called the tyranne of fishes).
O dissembling Curtesie! How fine this Tyrant Can tickle where she wounds?

s.def: The tyrant birds, members of the family Tyrannidae, which often fight or drive off other birds which approach their nests.
ex: The Tyrant... The courage of this little Bird is singular.

s.def: Tyrannical, tyrannous; like, characteristic of, or in the manner of a tyrant.
ex: He was most tirant & cruell of all emperours.
Thus must I from the smoake into the smother, From tyrant Duke, vnto a tyrant Brother.
...a reconciliation between our no longer parent state, but tyrant state, and these colonies.

s.def: To tyrannize.
To act like a tyrant; to be tyrannical.

ety: Attested in the sense “rim of a wheel” since ca. 1500. Generally considered to be a use of Middle English tir(e), a clipped byform of atir (“equipment, furnishings, ornament”), whence modern attire. A less accepted theory derives it from the verb to tie. The spelling tyre was predominant in the 16th century, but largely gave way to tire in the 17th and 18th, before it was revived again outside North America in the 19th century.

s.def: wheel covering
The ring-shaped protective covering around a wheel which is usually made of rubber or plastic composite and is either pneumatic or solid.
ex: pneumatic tyres
runflat tyres

s.def: The metal rim, or metal covering on a rim, of a (wooden or metal) wheel, usually of steel or formerly wrought iron, as found on (horse-drawn or railway) carriages and wagons and on locomotives.
ex: iron tyres for the coach and iron shoes for the horse
tyres and rails of steel, and every axle with roller bearings

s.def: To fit tyres to (a vehicle).
ex: The circular iron platform over there is used in the task of tyring the wheels, a warm job, too, by the way.

s.def: Curdled milk.
Attire.
ex: And feeble nature cloth'd with fleshly tyre

s.def: To adorn.

ety: From Latin Tyrus, from Ancient Greek Τύρος (Túros), from Phoenician 𐤑𐤓 (ṣr /⁠Ṣur⁠/, “rock”) (), after the rocky formation on which the town was originally built. Compare Aramaic טוּרָא / ܛܘܪܐ (ṭūrā, “mountain, high territory”), Akkadian 𒌷𒀫𒊒 (ᵁᴿᵁṣur-ru /⁠Ṣurru⁠/), Tarifit aẓru (“rock”), Central Atlas Tamazight ⴰⵥⵔⵓ (aẓru, “stone”), Proto-Semitic *ṯ̣Vrr- (“flint”). Cognate to Arabic صُور (ṣūr), Hebrew צוֹר (Tzor), Tiberian Hebrew צר (Ṣōr), Turkish Sur.

s.def: A city in Lebanon, a major port on the Levantine Sea that was a city-state in Phoenicia in antiquity and the capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem during the Middle Ages.
An unincorporated community in Austin Township, Sanilac County, Michigan, United States, named after the biblical Tyre.
A town and hamlet therein, in Seneca County, New York, United States, named after Tyre, Lebanon.

ety: Maybe ultimately from Celtic *tir (“land”), from Proto-Celtic *tīros from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”), i.e. "dry land".

s.def: A state in western Austria. Capital: Innsbruck.
A geographic region in Central Europe including the state of Tyrol in Austria and the regions of South Tyrol and Trentino in Italy.

ety: Borrowed from French tyrolienne.

s.def: A traditional folk dance of Tyrol.
The music for such a dance.
A part of the Mediterranean Sea off the western coast of Italy, bounded by Corsica and Sardinia (west), Tuscany, Lazio, Campania, and Calabria (east), and Sicily (south).

ety: From Greek τζατζίκι (tzatzíki), from Ottoman Turkish جاجیق (cacık). Doublet of cacik.

s.def: An appetizer made from yogurt, cucumber, garlic, olive oil and dill or mint; usually served with pita bread and as a meze

ety: From Greek τζουράς (tzourás), from Turkish cura.

s.def: A Greek long-necked fretted lute.
